Title: As New Era of Global Conflict Rages, Climate Change Turns the Prizes to Dust
URL: https://www.nakedcapitalism.com/2026/07/as-new-era-of-global-conflict-rages-climate-change-turns-the-prizes-to-dust.html
Time Published: 2026-07-27T10:00:20Z
Full Content:
The shifting pack ice, numbing temperatures, and powerful currents of the Antarctic’s Weddell Sea led Ernest Shackleton’s to describe it as the “worst portion of the worst sea in the world”. It made good on its reputation in 1915 when it sank Shackleton’s ship, Endurance, and those same conditions helped preserve it for more than a century. Discovered in 2022, Endurance is now becoming more accessible, however due to climate change. Those same climate forces making Shackleton’s ship easier to reach are also driving competition over shipping lanes and underwater minerals and fossil fuels. Indeed, many view global warming not as a threat, but as an opportunity. The Heritage Foundation, the crazy capitalist think tank responsible for Project 2025, argued in that screed that the NOAA’s work was “harmful to US prosperity.” And so away we go with Shackleton’s Endurance acting as a North Star. As the geopolitical wars rage over mineral and fossil fuel hot spots, and contests over shipping lanes and land corridors intensify, the world boils, ensuring that no one will emerge victorious aside from Mother Nature. A Vicious Spiral Let’s start near the opposite pole from Shackleton’s resting place where the competition over the Arctic heats up as the water literally does so. The journey from eastern China to England, which normally takes 40 days via the Suez Canal, more than 50 days around the Cape of Good Hope, and a complicated and expensive China-Europe rail route, can be cut in half by an accommodating Arctic route. As The Economist announces, “the Arctic will become more connected to the global economy.” That’s one way of putting it. Snow reflects 85 percent of the sunlight that hits it, exposed water only 7 percent. So as the Arctic melts, it speeds up the process for the remaining ice. The Arctic has been warming four times faster than anywhere else on the planet since 1979, according to multiple scientific studies. That means, according to a recent study in Communications Earth & Environment, that all ice-going vessels would only be unable to navigate this route in the spring come 2065, and that the route would be navigable year-round by 2100. Hooray! What often goes unmentioned in these pieces hyperventilating over how arctic shipping routes will transform the global economy is what exactly that means for the climate. And that’s not a pretty picture. Put simply, there won’t be much of a global economy left. Here are what some cities will look like as vessels breeze through the Arctic: If we want to really connect the Arctic to the economy, there’s always the ice-free future to consider. I imagine many/most of us look at those maps and recoil in horror. Project 2025 authors, capitalism’s most crazed supporters, and others cheerleading the expedited shipping through the Arctic see dollar signs. Needless to say, it’s not just sea level rise, but the breakdown of ocean circulation systems and weather patterns, bringing more severe weather, global food production collapse, and an inescapable doom loop. The Arctic’s increasing connection to the global economy is already helping to speed up the breakdown. From France24: It’s a vicious cycle. As sea ice melts and opens new routes for maritime traffic in the Arctic, the environmental fallout caused by vessels burning fossil fuels adds to global warming, which in turn melts more sea ice. A perfect example of this is black carbon. It’s a sooty material emitted from gas and diesel engines that aren’t completely combusted. Not only does black carbon pollute the air with particulate matter, but because of its ability to absorb light as heat, it contributes to climate change by warming the air. When black carbon is deposited on ice in the Arctic, it takes away its ability to reflect heat. “The black colour deposited on the white ice means the ice then absorbs more sunlight, leading to more melting,” explained Sammie Buzzard, a polar scientist at the Centre for Polar Observation and Modelling at Northumbria University. *** Elsewhere, similar geoeconomic battles are playing out over transit corridors that are likely to be rendered useless—or at least not worth the investment— by climate change. The Caspian Sea is currently a focal point of the Middle Corridor, to which the Trump Route for International peace and Prosperity aspires to link up to. The geopolitical contest over Central Asian minerals, control over the Caucasus, and energy flows from the Caspian region are seeing tensions rise and increase the risk of conflict. Meanwhile the Caspian Sea is dying. From SciTech Daily: Water levels in the Caspian Sea, the largest landlocked body of water in the world, are steadily falling as rising temperatures cause more evaporation than inflow. Even if global warming is kept below 2°C, scientists estimate the sea could drop by 5 to 10 meters. If temperatures rise further, the decline could reach up to 21 meters by the end of the century. In the northern Caspian, the findings show that some settlements, ports, and industrial facilities could end up being stranded tens or even hundreds of kilometers from new shorelines. The exposed dry seabed is likely to release dust containing industrial contaminants and salt, posing serious threats to human health, as previously occurred with the drying of the Aral Sea. The findings also predict a concerning trajectory for industry, with critical ports in all bordering countries being impacted. Baku (Azerbaijan), Anzali (Iran), and Aktau (Kazakhstan) are expected to experience increases in distance to shore of 1 km or more, while Turkmenbashi (Turkmenistan), and Lagan (Russia; planned future site), could see increases of 16 km and 115 km respectively… Some cities around the Caspian use desalination (removing salt and minerals from saltwater) for freshwater supplies, and water level declines are already impacting desalination operations at Aktau in Kazakhstan. Loss of water from the Caspian could also affect the regional climate, leading to reduced rainfall and drier conditions across central Asia with indirect impacts on agriculture. Further east where the “Great Game” is once again playing out, water is increasingly hard to come by, and it won’t be long before Mackinder’s Heartland Theory needs a Mad Max-style update. From IOP Science: The year 2025, designated by the United Nations as the ‘International Year of Glaciers’ Preservation’, ironically became the most negative glacier mass-balance year on record in Central Asia. In situobservations reveal exceptionally strong and spatially coherent ice losses across the region, although not all individual glaciers experienced record losses. Regional simulations with the Global Glacier Evolution Model support these findings, indicating that 64% of glaciers larger than 1 km2(∼4000 glaciers) reached their most negative annual mass balance within the study period. Within a single year, glaciers in Central Asia lost an estimated 30 ± 6 km3 of ice (26 ± 9 Gt), corresponding to ∼2% of their present-day total mass. Mass loss was strongest in the western Tien Shan and western Pamir (−2% to −4%) and more moderate in the eastern Tien Shan and eastern Pamir (−1% to −1.5%). Climate reanalysis attributes the extreme 2025 losses to persistently above-average spring and summer temperatures, an unusually early onset of the melt season, and reduced snowfall frequency during late spring and summer. Together, these conditions enhanced melt-amplifying feedbacks by accelerating snow loss, leading to earlier exposure of low-albedo ice surfaces. The 2025 losses mark an alarming milestone for Central Asian glaciers and may become the new normal in the future. To add a little more perspective, approximately 81 percent of Central Asia’s population depends on water originating in the Tien Shan and Pamir. And as supplies dwindle it increases the chances of internal destabilization and external conflict, which equals instability across food systems, energy markets, and regional trade. The Panama Canal This choke point is at the heart of the US and China struggle for control over global shipping infrastructure. Under pressure from Washington, Panama “retook control” of the Pacific Ocean port of Balboa and the Atlantic Ocean port of Cristobal after a court annulled a contract that had allowed a subsidiary of Hong Kong-based CK Hutchison Holdings to operate both since 1997. Beijing has retaliated by detaining Panama-flagged vessels, and Chinese shipping giant Cosco, which owns one of the world’s largest fleets of tankers, suspended operations at the two busiest Panama Canal ports. This fight is playing out following a Blackrock consortium’s attempt—with an assist from Washington—to buy up dozens of ports from CK Hutchison. Beijing has nixed the deal over concerns that the new ownership could, under direction from Washington, raise prices on or refuse Chinese ships or allow the US to militarize the ports and use them to enact a maritime blockade of China. Whoever ultimately controls the Panama ports might not have much to celebrate. The Panama Canal Authority is already reducing maximum navigable drafts in anticipation of the coming El Nino weather pattern. Under “normal” water level conditions, the Canal can handle 34 to 38 daily transits, but that had be cut by about 30 percent in 2023-24 due to the last El Nino when October 2023 saw the least amount of rainfall in recorded history. This upcoming El Nino is expected to be much worse. *** From where I sit, the fault for this race toward our own destruction lies almost exclusively in Washington and the transnational oligarchs it serves. By 05:49 GMT, Dow Jones futures had gained 398 points, or 0.8%, while S&P 500 futures were up 66 points, or 0.9%. Nasdaq 100 futures led the advance, climbing 406 points, or 1.4%. Monetary policy is also firmly in focus ahead of the Federal Reserve’s interest rate announcement on Wednesday. While inflation risks linked to the conflict in the Middle East remain under close scrutiny, futures markets continue to indicate that most investors expect policymakers to leave interest rates unchanged. Title: George Gibney due back before court for sentencing hearing
URL: https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/07/27/george-gibney-due-back-before-court-for-sentencing-hearing/
Time Published: 2026-07-27T08:51:49Z
Full Content:
A woman sexually abused by former swim coach George Gibney has said she gets to walk from court “free”, while the world will know him as a “convicted, serial paedophile”. She told the Central Criminal Court that his abuse of her some 50 years ago caused “more than just a loss of innocence”; it brought about the “destruction of a previously happy and healthy childhood”. “You were a person in authority. People respected and trusted you and you abused that position ... You took and took as you saw fit without a thought for the immediate or lifelong impact,” she told Gibney, who looked ahead into space from his wheelchair. The woman was one of four found by a jury to have been abused by the coach as girls between the ages of eight and 13 about 50 years ago. A jury earlier this month found the 78-year-old guilty of 39 counts of indecent assault and one count of attempted rape on dates between 1971 and 1981 at various locations, including at two swimming pools in south Co Dublin. The attempted rape took place in a changing room at Newpark Sports Centre in Blackrock, Dublin. [ The George Gibney trial: ‘Predatory’ abuser operated at heart of Irish swimmingOpens in new window ] Gibney’s senior counsel, Patrick Gageby, told the court on Monday that the former coach accepts the jury’s verdict and will not appeal against his convictions. “You have a very different person in front of you than the person who committed these offences against very young children in his care,” counsel said as part of submissions to Judge Mícheál O’Higgins during a sentencing hearing. The Director of Public Prosecutions contended that the offences fall within the upper range of offending due in part to Gibney’s authoritative position and the age of the victims. The judge said he would take time to consider the victim-impact statements delivered by the four victims. He remanded Gibney in custody pending sentencing in October. The trial heard Gibney gave some of the girls lifts to swimming and abused them in his car. Further abuse of two sisters happened in his home when they were babysitting his children. The assaults included French kissing, inappropriate touching, digital penetration and forced oral sex. In a victim-impact statement, one of the survivors said she needed psychological intervention from the age of nine, had nightmares, isolated herself and self-harmed due to his actions. Sports were a big part of her family, and swimming was her “absolute joy”. She said he robbed her potential and she never found out if she would have ended up a good, great or mediocre athlete. He changed the trajectory of her life, and “absolutely not in the ways I wanted”, she said. She had to watch him being “lauded” and “hero worshipped” by the establishment while knowing the truth about his “evilness”. “The world is going to know you now as a convicted serial paedophile, while I get to walk out of here free, free of you,” she said. Another survivor said she finally felt “safe and championed” after being believed by gardaí when she reported the abuse in recent years. She outlined to the court how her life has been negatively shaped by Gibney’s actions. She became “almost unreachable” and an “observer” who never fully participated in life. A third woman said her 13-year-old self has been “frozen in time” and she is not sure if she will ever be released. Her overwhelming emotion was anger at what Gibney did to her decades ago and how this has affected her relationships. She said the trial was “traumatising”, and she criticised press coverage of it. The law needs to be changed so it respects the dignity and courage of victims, she said. The fourth woman read a victim-impact statement but asked for her privacy to be respected. Gibney had been charged with 79 counts. At the outset of the trial he pleaded guilty to five counts of indecent assault, while the judge threw out 33 charges after the prosecution’s evidence was heard. The jury acquitted Gibney of one indecent assault count. Title: One-third of Seattle’s downtown is empty: Here’s how America’s boomtown turned into one of the toughest places to find a job
URL: https://fortune.com/2026/07/27/why-is-it-so-hard-to-find-a-job-in-seattle-office-vacancies-labor-market-minimum-wage/
Time Published: 2026-07-27T08:00:00Z
Full Content:
A decade ago, Seattle was the poster child of American tech prosperity. Amazon and Microsoft had turned a midsize Pacific Northwest city into a magnet for engineers, executives, and capital, adding roughly 40,000 jobs per year at the peak of the boom, according to the Puget Sound Regional Council. Today, more than one-third of downtown Seattle’s office space sits empty, its job postings have collapsed faster than almost any other U.S. metro, and even Starbucks—the coffee giant founded in the city in 1971—is shifting jobs south to Nashville, as it commits to a $100 million, 2,000-person new footprint in Music City. The story of Seattle’s reversal unfolds in three overlapping arcs: an office market in free fall, a labor market that has gone from boom to bust, and a policy environment that has made survival harder for the small businesses left behind. Seattle’s downtown office vacancy rate hit 35.6% in the fourth quarter of 2025, up from 32.3% a year earlier, according to Cushman & Wakefield data. That marks a stunning reversal from the pre-pandemic era: As recently as early 2025, the central business district’s availability rate—offices with departures pending—and vacancy rate were already hitting all-time highs based on CoStar data stretching back to 1982. Some brokers put the number even higher, with Colliers reporting vacancy touching 39.1% in late 2024 as remote work, tech layoffs, and cautious leasing decisions compounded. Office building values in the district have plunged sharply as a result, with landlords struggling to fill space abandoned by major tenants. The office crisis is inseparable from a broader collapse in hiring. Seattle metro job postings fell 35% between February 2020 and October 2025, the second-steepest drop of any major U.S. metro after San Francisco’s 37% decline, according to Axios’s analysis of Indeed data. Tech firms in the area have announced tens of thousands of job reductions since 2023, primarily driven by Microsoft, Amazon, and Blue Origin. The region posted a net loss of 13,000 jobs in 2025—its first annual decline since the pandemic and a stark reversal from the 40,000-job annual gains of the boom years. Into this contraction came a wage floor with no exceptions. Seattle’s minimum wage, $20.76 an hour and applied uniformly to all employers regardless of size since January 2025, has intensified pressure on small businesses trying to survive the downtown exodus. A peer-reviewed study published in Labour Economics found the wage ordinance’s announcement effect actually deterred new business formation within Seattle’s borders while generating positive “spillover” openings in neighboring suburbs, suggesting firms redirected growth rather than uniformly closing shop. Earlier University of Washington research similarly found the wage hikes reduced low-wage workers’ hours by about 9% even as hourly pay rose roughly 3%, per Ballotpedia’s fact-check compilation. What makes Seattle’s situation distinct from other regional slowdowns is how tightly these three arcs lock together. CoStar estimates Seattle won’t fully break out of the vacancy cycle before 2027—a timeline that assumes the feedback loop stops tightening, which so far it hasn’t. Pick a case and see what happened next. Company–incident pairs This site shows how share prices moved after an incident became public. It does not prove that the incident caused the move. Across the catalog The large number is the median difference between the company return and SPY. “Below SPY” is the share of cases that trailed the benchmark. These figures start at the pre-disclosure baseline rather than one shared post-incident entry point. Media context across the catalog We recovered written articles whose recorded headlines named the selected company during the first 14 days after disclosure. Selected cases AT&T disclosed that threat actors illegally downloaded call and text interaction records covering nearly all wireless customers for specified periods. The Change Healthcare ransomware attack disrupted US claims, pharmacy and payment infrastructure on a national scale. Microsoft disclosed that Midnight Blizzard accessed and exfiltrated email from a small percentage of corporate accounts, including senior leadership. Caesars disclosed a social-engineering attack through an outsourced IT support vendor that led to theft of loyalty-program customer data. MGM disclosed a cybersecurity issue that forced system shutdowns and disrupted hotel and casino operations across multiple US properties. Clorox disclosed unauthorized activity that forced systems offline and later caused widescale operational, order-processing and product-availability disruption. One important limit Earnings, company news and the wider market do not pause for a cyber incident. SPY gives us a consistent comparison, not a causal answer. Title: DCC board backs ‘compelling’ takeover bid of up to £5.73 billion
URL: https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/07/27/dcc-board-backs-compelling-takeover-bid-of-up-to-573-billion/
Time Published: 2026-07-27T06:46:45Z
Full Content:
DCC Energy chief executive Donal Murphy said he expects the vast majority of shareholders to support the sale of the group to two US private equity firms in a deal worth up to £5.73 billion (€6.71 billion). Murphy, though, finds himself on a collision course with some top investors resisting the deal. The Dublin-based group confirmed on Monday it had agreed to sell itself to KKR and Energy Capital. The transaction that includes a £65.25-a-share upfront payment and £1.25 extra per share if they achieve at least $800 million (€704 million) from a sale of the tech division, known as Nexora. The bid consortium had included the payment of DCC’s final €1.47-a-share dividend on its earnings for last year in each of the multiple offers it tabled since late April. The dividend was included in the statement on the agreed deal on Monday, even though it had actually been paid out last week. Murphy said this was to allow the market compare each offer from the time DCC rejected an initial €58-a-share bid. The proposal values the upfront cash offer at a 21.3 per cent premium to DCC’s closing share price in London – where it is listed – on April 28th, before it emerged that KKR and Energy Capital were circling the group. “We believe the majority of shareholders will vote in favour of this,” Murphy told The Irish Times, adding that the board had “engaged very robustly” with the suitors over the past three months. DCC is one of three Irish public companies subject to takeover proposals. PTSB and Irish Continental Group are also under offer. Murphy has overseen a strategy to abandon DCC’s conglomerate roots to focus on energy. He said that while the board “absolutely believes” the remaining energy division is on course to double its operating profit to £830 million between 2022 and 2030, the target is “not without risk” when weighted against an uncertain geopolitical and macroeconomic backdrop as well as the need for the group to invest £1 billion-£1.2 billion. “When the board looks at it and evaluates it in totality, we believe that this is very compelling from a shareholder perspective and that’s why we recommended it,” said Murphy. Five big shareholders – Fidelity International (FIL), DCC’s founder Jim Flavin, Aviva Investors, Marathon Asset Management and Ninety One – have signalled in recent times that they would not support an offer around the level tabled by the consortium. They own more than 15 per cent of the stock between them. Alex Wright, portfolio manager at FIL which owns 6.9 per cent of DCC, said on Monday that his position remains unchanged from earlier this month, when he said he would only entertain a bid of a least £70 a share. Flavin also said he would continue to campaign against a sale. DCC, whose businesses once spanned Robert Roberts tea and coffee to waste management, decided in late 2024 to abandon the remaining elements of its conglomerate roots. DCC sold its healthcare unit a year ago. It also offloaded part of its technology business, with the remainder of that division, Nexora, currently on the market and expected to be sold by the end of this year. Murphy said that despite extensive engagement with the market and the strategic progress DCC has made in recent years, the FTSE 100 company had not enjoyed an expected valuation bump in the public market. DCC – whose energy businesses span the operation of 1,173 petrol stations in Europe to distributing liquid gas on both sides of the Atlantic, and installing and maintaining solar PV and heat pump systems – had tweaked the narrative in efforts to secure a re-rating. While it once put greater emphasis on how it fit into the environment, social and governance (ESG) agenda as a play on the energy transition, it had put more weight recently on security and affordability of fuel supply, according to analysts. “The evidence has been that this transition is way, way, way slower than anyone anticipated. When we set out in 2022 with our strategy, we believed and the world believed that energy transition was going to happen very quickly. Energy transition is happening very slowly.” Murphy said DCC has faced difficulties attracting new investors in recent times as they have preferred to wait for evidence of how the energy strategy will evolve. DCC shares were up 1.2 per cent at £63.60 in late morning trading on Monday. Title: AI ETFs Have Now Become a $65 Billion Market
URL: https://www.thedailyupside.com/etf/thematics-sectors/ai-etfs-have-now-become-a-65-billion-market/
Time Published: 2026-07-27T04:03:00Z
Full Content:
Assets into funds that track the artificial intelligence segment have risen sharply since last year, per J.P. Morgan. Mallika Mitra Guest Contributor to The Daily Upside Oscar-winning actress Reese Witherspoon may have irked the internet when she said the artificial intelligence revolution has begun, but ETF investors are certainly hoping she’s right. Overall assets for thematic AI funds have skyrocketed in the past year, according to a recent report from J.P. Morgan Asset Management. While assets were at $10.3 billion a year ago, they hit $64.9 billion as of the end of June, according to data shared with ETF Upside. Artificial intelligence is now the top theme by AUM, followed by infrastructure, defense, cybersecurity and natural resources. The funds are a convenient vehicle for institutional money to trade broad exposure quickly with plenty of liquidity, said Erik Kratz, chief investment officer at Arena Private Wealth. But they also let passive-leaning investors feel active by targeting a theme without the concentration risk of a single stock. “We view these thematic ETFs as sentiment-driven vehicles rather than an ETF that will be found in future retirees’ portfolios in 30 years,” Kratz said. “Real wealth is still built by owning great businesses directly within a secular theme like AI, and holding them through the volatility, not by rotating through a basket.” Long-term plays or not, it’s no wonder that investors are excited to get exposure to the AI craze without having to commit to individual stocks, many of which have been volatile as investors weigh massive capital expenditures against potential returns. NVIDIA’s stock, for instance, sank to about $165 per share in April before soaring to above $230 in May. But AI has also helped accelerate a surge for thematic ETFs in general. Unlike previously popular niche funds like those focused on cannabis, these span many sectors including robotics, electric vehicles and data infrastructure: Sweet Home AI: Performance-wise, some of the most popular AI funds are doing their part to keep investors’ portfolios in the black. The iShares AI Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) is up around 30% year to date, while the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF (AIQ) is up around 15%. Value funds are holding the aerospace and satellite communications company despite a sky-high market capitalization. The US isn’t alone, as European Union members, Asian countries and Middle Eastern nations have all been boosting their defense budgets as well. Income exchange-traded funds are showing investors the money, and their popularity is showing no signs of slowing down. Tax efficiency, rather than investment strategy, could be what helps new funds stand out from the crowd. Chipmaker stocks have tanked in recent weeks. Nevertheless, inflows have persisted as investors bet on a rebound. The Robotics Supercycle ETF (RTOO) was launched alongside space- and defense-themed ETFs. Liquid alternative investment vehicles aren’t new, but their role in portfolios has changed in today’s concentrated equity markets. It might be time for financial advisors to give the rest of the market a second look. A proposed “event contracts” ETF would turn sports gambling into a diversified portfolio play if regulators sign off. SGOV from iShares may become the first ETF in its class to reach $100 billion in assets. Morningstar’s Kenneth Lamont said thematic ETFs “appeal to investors’ worst instincts.” Subversive ETFs filed to launch two funds that specifically exclude companies associated with the world’s richest man. © 2026 The Daily Upside

Summit Tokyo」を共同開催しました。 当日は、金融機関、資産運用会社、暗号資産交換業者、ブロックチェーンインフラ企業、web3プロジェクトなど、多様なバックグラウンドを持つ参加者が来場し、会場は終日活発な議論と交流で賑わいました。 各セッションでは、グローバル・ステーブルコイン戦略、スポットETF、クロスボーダー決済、機関投資家向けカストディ、暗号資産交換業の将来、RWA（Real Jonathan Chang 氏 トラストレス・ビットコイン・ヴォールト — カストディを手放さないネイティブBTC担保 Babylon Labs CTO Vitalis Salis 氏 なお、本イベントで実施した各セッションの詳細については、セッションレポートとして順次公開予定です。 各登壇者による議論の内容や注目ポイントを詳しくご紹介します。 今回のイベントでは、以下のような市場トレンドが共通テーマとして挙げられました。 機関投資家によるデジタルアセット市場への参入拡大 ステーブルコインを活用した決済・送金インフラの高度化 トークン化資産（RWA）の実用フェーズへの移行 ビットコインを担保とした新たな金融サービスの発展 日本市場への期待と、グローバル市場との連携強化 厳選された国内外の意思決定者や実務責任者が一堂に会し、日本市場の将来像について率直な議論と活発な交流が行われました。 今年の議論を通じて共通していたテーマは、日本のデジタルアセット市場が「制度設計・PoC（実証実験）」の段階から、「社会実装・事業化」へと着実に移行し始めているということです。数年前までは「規制が整うか」が中心的な論点でしたが、現在では「どのような金融商品・サービスを、どのインフラ上で提供するか」が議論の中心となり、実装を前提とした具体的な議論が数多く交わされました。 特に、ステーブルコイン、トークン化資産（RWA）、機関投資家向けカストディ、Bitcoinを活用した新たな金融インフラ、そしてETF・トークン化ファンドなど、従来は個別に語られてきたテーマが、一つの金融エコシステムとして議論されたことは象徴的でした。デジタルアセットは単独のプロダクトではなく、決済・資産運用・市場インフラ・担保・流動性を横断する金融基盤として捉えられ始めており、日本市場もその転換点を迎えています。 また、多くの海外プロジェクトからは、日本市場への期待の高さもうかがえました。制度の明確性や金融機関との協業環境を評価する声が多く聞かれ、イベント当日は金融機関、Web3プロジェクト、インフラ企業、投資家による数多くの1on1ミーティングやネットワーキングが実施されました。単なる情報交換に留まらず、新たなPoCや事業提携、国内展開に向けた具体的な協議へと発展する対話が各所で生まれ、日本がグローバルデジタルアセット市場における重要な拠点として存在感を高めつつあることを印象付けました。 The Capital Summit Tokyoは、最新トレンドを共有する場であると同時に、日本と世界をつなぎ、新たな事業やパートナーシップが生まれるためのプラットフォームとして開催されました。DeFimansは今後も国内外のプレイヤーを結び付ける場を創出し、日本のデジタルアセット市場の発展とグローバルエコシステムとの接続に貢献してまいります。 ▪️タイトルスポンサー Tether（テザー）は、世界最大のステーブルコインであるUSDTの発行会社です。流通額は1,800億米ドルを超え、日々の決済ボリュームは大手カードネットワークに匹敵する規模を誇ります。デジタル金融における支配的な決済資産であり、新興国におけるドル資金フローの主要な決済インフラとしての役割を担っています。 ウェブサイト: tether.to ▪️ゴールドスポンサー RWA（Real World Assets）やオンチェーン金融向けに開発された、機関投資家向けLayer 1ブロックチェーンです。コンプライアンス対応、高い処理性能、既存の金融インフラとの相互運用性を重視して設計されています。 ウェブサイト: pharos.xyz Babylon Labsは、世界初のトラストレスかつセルフカストディ型のビットコインステーキングプロトコルを開発しました。これにより、ビットコイン保有者は、PoSチェーン、L2、データアベイラビリティ（DA）レイヤーなどのプルーフ・オブ・ステーク（PoS）システム上でBTCをステーキングでき、第三者によるカストディ、ブリッジソリューション、ラッピングサービスなしで、ステーキング報酬を得ることが可能になります。 ウェブサイト：https://babylonlabs.io/ ▪️シルバースポンサー Title: Oil asset protection projected to boost licensing round success
URL: https://punchng.com/oil-asset-protection-projected-to-boost-licensing-round-success/
Time Published: 2026-07-27T00:54:24Z
Full Content:
Most Widely Read Newspaper Kindly share this story: Nigeria’s ambitious 2025 oil licensing round is expected to benefit from sustained oil asset protection, as stakeholders emphasise pipeline security and Niger Delta stability to attract investment, DARE OLAWIN writes The country’s 2025 upstream oil licensing round has set ambitious production and reserve targets, with the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission seeking to add 500 million barrels to the country’s reserves and increase crude oil production by 300,000 barrels per day within three years. Industry stakeholders say achieving those objectives will depend not only on attracting investment but also on protecting oil assets, tackling crude oil theft, and maintaining stability in the Niger Delta. The 2025 licensing round underscores Nigeria’s efforts to strengthen upstream investment and expand exploration activities. According to the NUPRC, 143 companies submitted 200 bids for 37 of the 50 blocks offered during the commercial bid phase. The regulator expects the exercise to support reserve growth and increase production over the next three years. Stakeholders, however, argue that increased investment must be matched by improved protection of oil infrastructure, as pipeline vandalism and crude oil theft remain key challenges to production growth. They also stress the importance of assigning surveillance responsibilities to organisations with experience in protecting oil assets. The Federal Government engaged Tantita Security Services Nigeria Ltd to support the protection of oil assets and enhance security across parts of the Niger Delta. President Bola Tinubu appointed Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited, led by High Chief Government Ekpemupolo, alias Tompolo, to help safeguard Nigeria’s oil assets in the region. The company works alongside other security agencies in carrying out surveillance activities aimed at protecting oil facilities and supporting stability in the Niger Delta. Stakeholders say improved surveillance has contributed to efforts to reduce pipeline vandalism and crude oil theft while supporting more stable production levels. They also argue that protecting oil infrastructure remains critical to sustaining investment, improving production and supporting government revenue. The Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise, Muda Yusuf, said Nigeria’s energy transition agenda makes it important to secure existing oil assets while expanding production. He described the 2025 licensing round as an effort to strengthen the country’s energy sector but said improved security must accompany investment initiatives. “We are in the age of energy transition. NUPRC’s operation in this exercise is good for the economy. It will boost foreign reserves, firm up the naira and macroeconomic environment while deepening foreign capital inflows to the domestic economy,” he said. Yusuf added that stronger protection of oil and gas infrastructure could encourage additional investment in the sector. “The new momentum generated will help build capacity to increase the level of production in the oil and gas industry,” he added. Abuja-based energy expert Steven Martins said the outcome of the licensing round represented more than a routine administrative exercise, noting that sustaining oil asset protection would be important as new investments move into the operational phase. “It represents a strategic recalibration of Nigeria’s energy ambitions at a time when global markets are shifting rapidly, and the country faces pressure to strengthen production, attract capital, and reposition itself in the era of energy transition. “As NUPRC is looking forward to harvesting an additional 500 million barrels to the national crude oil reserve from the 2025 bid round, these extra barrels are expected to be driven by the commencement of operational activities of the 31 companies that emerged as winners of 37 oil and gas blocks in the bid round licensing. Protection of oil assets should also form part of the priority areas for stakeholders, and that is where TSSNL should always be supported to achieve its goals,” he said. Martins explained that the awarded assets span several producing and frontier basins, including 16 Niger Delta Onshore blocks, 18 Niger Delta Shallow Water blocks, one Niger Delta Deep Offshore block, three Benin Basin Onshore blocks, four Anambra Basin Onshore blocks, four Chad Basin Onshore blocks and four Benue Trough blocks. The Chief Executive Officer, NUPRC, Mrs Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, said at the Commercial Bid Conference for the Nigeria Licensing Round, themed “Expanding Opportunities: Right Play, Right Place, Right Time”, that the assets on offer have significant reserve potential. “The assets available in this licensing round have potential to add about 500 million barrels to Nigeria’s reserves, increasing our existing reserves of crude oil and condensate—which currently stand at 37.01 billion barrels—and 215.19 trillion cubic feet of gas,” she said. Eyesan said the absence of bids for the 13 frontier blocks was not unexpected. According to her, the assets presented during the 2025 commercial bid had previously been recovered from operators, while the commission would continue assessing other assets for possible inclusion in future licensing exercises. “The reason why we are in the market is because of the blocks that we have recovered from existing operators,” she said. Industry analysts also noted that the licensing round attracted notable investor interest in frontier basins. Some winners The companies that emerged as winners of the 2025 Licensing Round include SSonic Petroleum Limited (PPL 2A29), CFP Pipeline and Flowlines (2A30), Dutchford E&P Limited (2A32), Attabanson Global Company Limited (2A33 and PPL 901), Rosem Energy Limited (2A38), and Pivot-GIS Limited (2A39). The others include Network E&P (2A40), Asharami (2A41), LexOil (2A42), BVOF (2A43), GupscoEnergy Limited (2A44 and 2A51), Saratoga (2A45), Volante (2A46), Concept-Reel Petroleum Services Limited (2A47 and 2A55), Clinton Oil Field (2A48 and 2A62), Nuway Oaklane Limited (2A49), Ramec (2A50), Italia (2A53), Blueridge E&P (2A54), Up Energies Limited (2A56), and AYM Shafa (2A57). There are also Blackrock Holdings Limited (2A58), Funtay Integrated Business Limited (2A59), Riparian Development and Production Limited (2A60), Nikstallis (2A61 and PPL 900), Stardeep Petroleum (PPL 2010), Dakoda & U Limited (PPL 308 and PPL 800), Southborne Oil and Gas Limited (PPL 902), Lanaka Petroleum (PPL 903), Highban Resources Limited (PPL 700) and Eyre Energy Limited (PPL 801). Views from stakeholders Stakeholders have continued to emphasise the importance of pipeline protection to Nigeria’s oil production ambitions, arguing that safeguarding critical infrastructure remains essential to sustaining output, attracting investment and supporting broader economic growth. Related News Over 1,100 host community projects ongoing in Niger Delta, says NUPRC Oil block bidding: Inside Nigeria’s seven-hour transparency test REAN urges action to accelerate Nigeria’s clean energy transition In a published report, the President-General of the Niger Delta Progressive Alliance, Nse Udoh, argued that pipeline surveillance has helped national institutions move from reactive crisis management to more strategic planning and long-term decision-making. “It is important to clarify the role of pipeline surveillance within the wider energy landscape. Energy security encompasses the full value chain, from exploration and production to refining, distribution, pricing policy, and subsidy frameworks. Pipeline surveillance does not manage these domains,” he said. Udoh, however, maintained that pipeline surveillance plays a critical supporting role by protecting infrastructure that transports petroleum resources. “Its mandate is precise: safeguarding critical infrastructure that transports petroleum resources. Yet this single function has proven foundational. Without secure transportation channels, production targets falter, refining plans collapse, exports decline, and fiscal projections become unreliable,” he added. He further argued that asset protection underpins the efficient operation of the petroleum value chain. “Asset protection, in this context, is not a supporting activity. It is a precondition for economic order. In effect, the pipeline is the hinge on which the entire petroleum value chain turns. When that hinge is weak, every other link in the chain carries strain. When it is secure, the entire system gains coherence,” he wrote. According to him, sustained monitoring and rapid-response measures have contributed to fewer pipeline breaches and incidents of illegal tapping, while improvements in production have helped strengthen Nigeria’s position in the international oil market. Udoh also argued that greater certainty in crude oil transportation supports planning across the petroleum value chain. “Economic stability follows predictability. When crude flows are secure, refineries can plan feedstock intake with assurance. Export commitments can be met without fear of sudden shortfalls. Gas-to-power projects can operate without recurrent shutdown risks. “Investors can assess Nigeria’s petroleum sector with clearer risk profiles. Surveillance therefore does more than stop theft. It reintroduces reliability into national energy planning. And reliability is the bedrock upon which sustainable economic growth is built. “With predictable flows, national budgeting becomes more credible, infrastructure planning becomes more precise, and long-term contracts become easier to negotiate. Predictability is the silent currency of modern economies, and pipeline surveillance has begun restoring it,” he stated. He added that improved production accountability has supported export earnings, strengthened foreign exchange inflows and enhanced fiscal capacity, while helping national oil company operations become more efficient through lower losses and improved operational continuity. According to Udoh, more stable revenues also improve government planning by creating greater fiscal certainty and supporting investment in infrastructure, social services and economic diversification. Traditional rulers and community leaders in the Niger Delta have also called for continued support for Tantita Security Services Limited following a vote of confidence passed on the company by the National Assembly. The leaders said the company’s involvement in protecting oil and gas pipelines had coincided with improvements in security across some oil-producing communities, while also creating employment opportunities for young people. Commenting on the development, the President-General of the Isoko Development Union, Christopher Akpotu, commended the joint committee of the Senate and House of Representatives for dismissing petitions filed against the company. He described the decision as beneficial to the Niger Delta and urged stakeholders to focus on expanding opportunities in the oil and gas sector rather than internal disputes. “That is the right way to go,” he said. “There are many opportunities in the oil and gas sector. We should focus on how to derive more benefits rather than fighting over what has already been allocated.” Akpotu cautioned that prolonged disagreements among host communities could create opportunities for outsiders to benefit at their expense. “At the end of the day, if we continue fighting, we give room to those who have no stake in our communities to take what rightfully belongs to us,” he added. While acknowledging concerns about the distribution of benefits, he maintained that the surveillance contract had positively affected many communities. “The truth is that many communities and youths have benefited from the surveillance contract. It may not be evenly distributed, but the impact is evident,” he said. He also urged Tantita to broaden engagement with traditional rulers, youths and community leaders to promote fairness and strengthen long-term cooperation. Similarly, the President-General of the Ughelli Descendants Union, Sam Akpemegi, said security had improved since the company began operations, noting that both physical surveillance and intelligence-driven strategies had been deployed. “They have done very well and improved security since they began operations,” he said, adding that the company’s activities now extend across many communities. Akpemegi added that the company’s presence had benefited both traditional institutions and local residents, while calling for continued support for its operations. In the same vein, the Odiologbo of Ofagbe Kingdom, Ogaga Ikpoku, backed the National Assembly’s decision, describing it as timely and beneficial to peace and stability in the region. Stakeholders also argued that improved protection of oil assets has produced environmental and social benefits in parts of the Niger Delta. They noted that illegal refining and pipeline sabotage had previously polluted waterways, degraded farmlands and exposed communities to environmental and security risks, adding that sustained surveillance efforts against illegal refining sites and repeated pipeline breaches have supported ongoing environmental recovery. There are also Blackrock Holdings Limited (2A58), Funtay Integrated Business Limited (2A59), Riparian Development and Production Limited (2A60), Nikstallis (2A61 and PPL 900), Stardeep Petroleum (PPL 2010), Dakoda & U Limited (PPL 308 and PPL 800), Southborne Oil and Gas Limited (PPL 902), Lanaka Petroleum (PPL 903), Highban Resources Limited (PPL 700) and Eyre Energy Limited (PPL 801). Views from stakeholders Stakeholders have continued to emphasise the importance of pipeline protection to Nigeria’s oil production ambitions, arguing that safeguarding critical infrastructure remains essential to sustaining output, attracting investment and supporting broader economic growth. Related News Over 1,100 host community projects ongoing in Niger Delta, says NUPRC Oil block bidding: Inside Nigeria’s seven-hour transparency test REAN urges action to accelerate Nigeria’s clean energy transition In a published report, the President-General of the Niger Delta Progressive Alliance, Nse Udoh, argued that pipeline surveillance has helped national institutions move from reactive crisis management to more strategic planning and long-term decision-making. “It is important to clarify the role of pipeline surveillance within the wider energy landscape. Energy security encompasses the full value chain, from exploration and production to refining, distribution, pricing policy, and subsidy frameworks. Pipeline surveillance does not manage these domains,” he said. Udoh, however, maintained that pipeline surveillance plays a critical supporting role by protecting infrastructure that transports petroleum resources. “Its mandate is precise: safeguarding critical infrastructure that transports petroleum resources. Yet this single function has proven foundational. Without secure transportation channels, production targets falter, refining plans collapse, exports decline, and fiscal projections become unreliable,” he added. He further argued that asset protection underpins the efficient operation of the petroleum value chain. “Asset protection, in this context, is not a supporting activity. It is a precondition for economic order. In effect, the pipeline is the hinge on which the entire petroleum value chain turns. When that hinge is weak, every other link in the chain carries strain. When it is secure, the entire system gains coherence,” he wrote. According to him, sustained monitoring and rapid-response measures have contributed to fewer pipeline breaches and incidents of illegal tapping, while improvements in production have helped strengthen Nigeria’s position in the international oil market. Udoh also argued that greater certainty in crude oil transportation supports planning across the petroleum value chain. “Economic stability follows predictability. When crude flows are secure, refineries can plan feedstock intake with assurance. Export commitments can be met without fear of sudden shortfalls. Gas-to-power projects can operate without recurrent shutdown risks. “Investors can assess Nigeria’s petroleum sector with clearer risk profiles. Surveillance therefore does more than stop theft. It reintroduces reliability into national energy planning. And reliability is the bedrock upon which sustainable economic growth is built. “With predictable flows, national budgeting becomes more credible, infrastructure planning becomes more precise, and long-term contracts become easier to negotiate. Predictability is the silent currency of modern economies, and pipeline surveillance has begun restoring it,” he stated. He added that improved production accountability has supported export earnings, strengthened foreign exchange inflows and enhanced fiscal capacity, while helping national oil company operations become more efficient through lower losses and improved operational continuity. According to Udoh, more stable revenues also improve government planning by creating greater fiscal certainty and supporting investment in infrastructure, social services and economic diversification. Traditional rulers and community leaders in the Niger Delta have also called for continued support for Tantita Security Services Limited following a vote of confidence passed on the company by the National Assembly. The leaders said the company’s involvement in protecting oil and gas pipelines had coincided with improvements in security across some oil-producing communities, while also creating employment opportunities for young people. Commenting on the development, the President-General of the Isoko Development Union, Christopher Akpotu, commended the joint committee of the Senate and House of Representatives for dismissing petitions filed against the company. He described the decision as beneficial to the Niger Delta and urged stakeholders to focus on expanding opportunities in the oil and gas sector rather than internal disputes. “That is the right way to go,” he said. “There are many opportunities in the oil and gas sector. We should focus on how to derive more benefits rather than fighting over what has already been allocated.” Akpotu cautioned that prolonged disagreements among host communities could create opportunities for outsiders to benefit at their expense. “At the end of the day, if we continue fighting, we give room to those who have no stake in our communities to take what rightfully belongs to us,” he added. While acknowledging concerns about the distribution of benefits, he maintained that the surveillance contract had positively affected many communities. “The truth is that many communities and youths have benefited from the surveillance contract. It may not be evenly distributed, but the impact is evident,” he said. He also urged Tantita to broaden engagement with traditional rulers, youths and community leaders to promote fairness and strengthen long-term cooperation. Similarly, the President-General of the Ughelli Descendants Union, Sam Akpemegi, said security had improved since the company began operations, noting that both physical surveillance and intelligence-driven strategies had been deployed. “They have done very well and improved security since they began operations,” he said, adding that the company’s activities now extend across many communities. Akpemegi added that the company’s presence had benefited both traditional institutions and local residents, while calling for continued support for its operations. In the same vein, the Odiologbo of Ofagbe Kingdom, Ogaga Ikpoku, backed the National Assembly’s decision, describing it as timely and beneficial to peace and stability in the region. Stakeholders also argued that improved protection of oil assets has produced environmental and social benefits in parts of the Niger Delta. They noted that illegal refining and pipeline sabotage had previously polluted waterways, degraded farmlands and exposed communities to environmental and security risks, adding that sustained surveillance efforts against illegal refining sites and repeated pipeline breaches have supported ongoing environmental recovery. The 2025 licensing round underscores Nigeria’s efforts to strengthen upstream investment and expand exploration activities. According to the NUPRC, 143 companies submitted 200 bids for 37 of the 50 blocks offered during the commercial bid phase. The regulator expects the exercise to support reserve growth and increase production over the next three years. Stakeholders, however, argue that increased investment must be matched by improved protection of oil infrastructure, as pipeline vandalism and crude oil theft remain key challenges to production growth. They also stress the importance of assigning surveillance responsibilities to organisations with experience in protecting oil assets. The Federal Government engaged Tantita Security Services Nigeria Ltd to support the protection of oil assets and enhance security across parts of the Niger Delta. President Bola Tinubu appointed Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited, led by High Chief Government Ekpemupolo, alias Tompolo, to help safeguard Nigeria’s oil assets in the region. The company works alongside other security agencies in carrying out surveillance activities aimed at protecting oil facilities and supporting stability in the Niger Delta. Stakeholders say improved surveillance has contributed to efforts to reduce pipeline vandalism and crude oil theft while supporting more stable production levels. They also argue that protecting oil infrastructure remains critical to sustaining investment, improving production and supporting government revenue. The Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise, Muda Yusuf, said Nigeria’s energy transition agenda makes it important to secure existing oil assets while expanding production. He described the 2025 licensing round as an effort to strengthen the country’s energy sector but said improved security must accompany investment initiatives. “We are in the age of energy transition. NUPRC’s operation in this exercise is good for the economy. It will boost foreign reserves, firm up the naira and macroeconomic environment while deepening foreign capital inflows to the domestic economy,” he said. Yusuf added that stronger protection of oil and gas infrastructure could encourage additional investment in the sector. “The new momentum generated will help build capacity to increase the level of production in the oil and gas industry,” he added. Abuja-based energy expert Steven Martins said the outcome of the licensing round represented more than a routine administrative exercise, noting that sustaining oil asset protection would be important as new investments move into the operational phase. “It represents a strategic recalibration of Nigeria’s energy ambitions at a time when global markets are shifting rapidly, and the country faces pressure to strengthen production, attract capital, and reposition itself in the era of energy transition. “As NUPRC is looking forward to harvesting an additional 500 million barrels to the national crude oil reserve from the 2025 bid round, these extra barrels are expected to be driven by the commencement of operational activities of the 31 companies that emerged as winners of 37 oil and gas blocks in the bid round licensing. Protection of oil assets should also form part of the priority areas for stakeholders, and that is where TSSNL should always be supported to achieve its goals,” he said. Martins explained that the awarded assets span several producing and frontier basins, including 16 Niger Delta Onshore blocks, 18 Niger Delta Shallow Water blocks, one Niger Delta Deep Offshore block, three Benin Basin Onshore blocks, four Anambra Basin Onshore blocks, four Chad Basin Onshore blocks and four Benue Trough blocks. The Chief Executive Officer, NUPRC, Mrs Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, said at the Commercial Bid Conference for the Nigeria Licensing Round, themed “Expanding Opportunities: Right Play, Right Place, Right Time”, that the assets on offer have significant reserve potential. “The assets available in this licensing round have potential to add about 500 million barrels to Nigeria’s reserves, increasing our existing reserves of crude oil and condensate—which currently stand at 37.01 billion barrels—and 215.19 trillion cubic feet of gas,” she said. Eyesan said the absence of bids for the 13 frontier blocks was not unexpected. According to her, the assets presented during the 2025 commercial bid had previously been recovered from operators, while the commission would continue assessing other assets for possible inclusion in future licensing exercises. “The reason why we are in the market is because of the blocks that we have recovered from existing operators,” she said. Industry analysts also noted that the licensing round attracted notable investor interest in frontier basins. Some winners The companies that emerged as winners of the 2025 Licensing Round include SSonic Petroleum Limited (PPL 2A29), CFP Pipeline and Flowlines (2A30), Dutchford E&P Limited (2A32), Attabanson Global Company Limited (2A33 and PPL 901), Rosem Energy Limited (2A38), and Pivot-GIS Limited (2A39). The others include Network E&P (2A40), Asharami (2A41), LexOil (2A42), BVOF (2A43), GupscoEnergy Limited (2A44 and 2A51), Saratoga (2A45), Volante (2A46), Concept-Reel Petroleum Services Limited (2A47 and 2A55), Clinton Oil Field (2A48 and 2A62), Nuway Oaklane Limited (2A49), Ramec (2A50), Italia (2A53), Blueridge E&P (2A54), Up Energies Limited (2A56), and AYM Shafa (2A57). There are also Blackrock Holdings Limited (2A58), Funtay Integrated Business Limited (2A59), Riparian Development and Production Limited (2A60), Nikstallis (2A61 and PPL 900), Stardeep Petroleum (PPL 2010), Dakoda & U Limited (PPL 308 and PPL 800), Southborne Oil and Gas Limited (PPL 902), Lanaka Petroleum (PPL 903), Highban Resources Limited (PPL 700) and Eyre Energy Limited (PPL 801). According to him, sustained monitoring and rapid-response measures have contributed to fewer pipeline breaches and incidents of illegal tapping, while improvements in production have helped strengthen Nigeria’s position in the international oil market. Udoh also argued that greater certainty in crude oil transportation supports planning across the petroleum value chain. “Economic stability follows predictability. When crude flows are secure, refineries can plan feedstock intake with assurance. Export commitments can be met without fear of sudden shortfalls. Gas-to-power projects can operate without recurrent shutdown risks. “Investors can assess Nigeria’s petroleum sector with clearer risk profiles. Surveillance therefore does more than stop theft. It reintroduces reliability into national energy planning. And reliability is the bedrock upon which sustainable economic growth is built. “With predictable flows, national budgeting becomes more credible, infrastructure planning becomes more precise, and long-term contracts become easier to negotiate. Predictability is the silent currency of modern economies, and pipeline surveillance has begun restoring it,” he stated. He added that improved production accountability has supported export earnings, strengthened foreign exchange inflows and enhanced fiscal capacity, while helping national oil company operations become more efficient through lower losses and improved operational continuity. According to Udoh, more stable revenues also improve government planning by creating greater fiscal certainty and supporting investment in infrastructure, social services and economic diversification. Traditional rulers and community leaders in the Niger Delta have also called for continued support for Tantita Security Services Limited following a vote of confidence passed on the company by the National Assembly. The leaders said the company’s involvement in protecting oil and gas pipelines had coincided with improvements in security across some oil-producing communities, while also creating employment opportunities for young people. Commenting on the development, the President-General of the Isoko Development Union, Christopher Akpotu, commended the joint committee of the Senate and House of Representatives for dismissing petitions filed against the company. He described the decision as beneficial to the Niger Delta and urged stakeholders to focus on expanding opportunities in the oil and gas sector rather than internal disputes. “That is the right way to go,” he said. “There are many opportunities in the oil and gas sector. We should focus on how to derive more benefits rather than fighting over what has already been allocated.” Akpotu cautioned that prolonged disagreements among host communities could create opportunities for outsiders to benefit at their expense. “At the end of the day, if we continue fighting, we give room to those who have no stake in our communities to take what rightfully belongs to us,” he added. While acknowledging concerns about the distribution of benefits, he maintained that the surveillance contract had positively affected many communities. “The truth is that many communities and youths have benefited from the surveillance contract. It may not be evenly distributed, but the impact is evident,” he said. He also urged Tantita to broaden engagement with traditional rulers, youths and community leaders to promote fairness and strengthen long-term cooperation. Similarly, the President-General of the Ughelli Descendants Union, Sam Akpemegi, said security had improved since the company began operations, noting that both physical surveillance and intelligence-driven strategies had been deployed. “They have done very well and improved security since they began operations,” he said, adding that the company’s activities now extend across many communities. Akpemegi added that the company’s presence had benefited both traditional institutions and local residents, while calling for continued support for its operations. In the same vein, the Odiologbo of Ofagbe Kingdom, Ogaga Ikpoku, backed the National Assembly’s decision, describing it as timely and beneficial to peace and stability in the region. Stakeholders also argued that improved protection of oil assets has produced environmental and social benefits in parts of the Niger Delta. They noted that illegal refining and pipeline sabotage had previously polluted waterways, degraded farmlands and exposed communities to environmental and security risks, adding that sustained surveillance efforts against illegal refining sites and repeated pipeline breaches have supported ongoing environmental recovery. The company works alongside other security agencies in carrying out surveillance activities aimed at protecting oil facilities and supporting stability in the Niger Delta. Stakeholders say improved surveillance has contributed to efforts to reduce pipeline vandalism and crude oil theft while supporting more stable production levels. They also argue that protecting oil infrastructure remains critical to sustaining investment, improving production and supporting government revenue. The Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise, Muda Yusuf, said Nigeria’s energy transition agenda makes it important to secure existing oil assets while expanding production. He described the 2025 licensing round as an effort to strengthen the country’s energy sector but said improved security must accompany investment initiatives. “We are in the age of energy transition. NUPRC’s operation in this exercise is good for the economy. It will boost foreign reserves, firm up the naira and macroeconomic environment while deepening foreign capital inflows to the domestic economy,” he said. Yusuf added that stronger protection of oil and gas infrastructure could encourage additional investment in the sector. “The new momentum generated will help build capacity to increase the level of production in the oil and gas industry,” he added. Abuja-based energy expert Steven Martins said the outcome of the licensing round represented more than a routine administrative exercise, noting that sustaining oil asset protection would be important as new investments move into the operational phase. “It represents a strategic recalibration of Nigeria’s energy ambitions at a time when global markets are shifting rapidly, and the country faces pressure to strengthen production, attract capital, and reposition itself in the era of energy transition. “As NUPRC is looking forward to harvesting an additional 500 million barrels to the national crude oil reserve from the 2025 bid round, these extra barrels are expected to be driven by the commencement of operational activities of the 31 companies that emerged as winners of 37 oil and gas blocks in the bid round licensing. Protection of oil assets should also form part of the priority areas for stakeholders, and that is where TSSNL should always be supported to achieve its goals,” he said. Martins explained that the awarded assets span several producing and frontier basins, including 16 Niger Delta Onshore blocks, 18 Niger Delta Shallow Water blocks, one Niger Delta Deep Offshore block, three Benin Basin Onshore blocks, four Anambra Basin Onshore blocks, four Chad Basin Onshore blocks and four Benue Trough blocks. The Chief Executive Officer, NUPRC, Mrs Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, said at the Commercial Bid Conference for the Nigeria Licensing Round, themed “Expanding Opportunities: Right Play, Right Place, Right Time”, that the assets on offer have significant reserve potential. “The assets available in this licensing round have potential to add about 500 million barrels to Nigeria’s reserves, increasing our existing reserves of crude oil and condensate—which currently stand at 37.01 billion barrels—and 215.19 trillion cubic feet of gas,” she said. Eyesan said the absence of bids for the 13 frontier blocks was not unexpected. According to her, the assets presented during the 2025 commercial bid had previously been recovered from operators, while the commission would continue assessing other assets for possible inclusion in future licensing exercises. “The reason why we are in the market is because of the blocks that we have recovered from existing operators,” she said. Industry analysts also noted that the licensing round attracted notable investor interest in frontier basins. Some winners The companies that emerged as winners of the 2025 Licensing Round include SSonic Petroleum Limited (PPL 2A29), CFP Pipeline and Flowlines (2A30), Dutchford E&P Limited (2A32), Attabanson Global Company Limited (2A33 and PPL 901), Rosem Energy Limited (2A38), and Pivot-GIS Limited (2A39). The others include Network E&P (2A40), Asharami (2A41), LexOil (2A42), BVOF (2A43), GupscoEnergy Limited (2A44 and 2A51), Saratoga (2A45), Volante (2A46), Concept-Reel Petroleum Services Limited (2A47 and 2A55), Clinton Oil Field (2A48 and 2A62), Nuway Oaklane Limited (2A49), Ramec (2A50), Italia (2A53), Blueridge E&P (2A54), Up Energies Limited (2A56), and AYM Shafa (2A57). There are also Blackrock Holdings Limited (2A58), Funtay Integrated Business Limited (2A59), Riparian Development and Production Limited (2A60), Nikstallis (2A61 and PPL 900), Stardeep Petroleum (PPL 2010), Dakoda & U Limited (PPL 308 and PPL 800), Southborne Oil and Gas Limited (PPL 902), Lanaka Petroleum (PPL 903), Highban Resources Limited (PPL 700) and Eyre Energy Limited (PPL 801). Views from stakeholders Stakeholders have continued to emphasise the importance of pipeline protection to Nigeria’s oil production ambitions, arguing that safeguarding critical infrastructure remains essential to sustaining output, attracting investment and supporting broader economic growth. Martins explained that the awarded assets span several producing and frontier basins, including 16 Niger Delta Onshore blocks, 18 Niger Delta Shallow Water blocks, one Niger Delta Deep Offshore block, three Benin Basin Onshore blocks, four Anambra Basin Onshore blocks, four Chad Basin Onshore blocks and four Benue Trough blocks. The Chief Executive Officer, NUPRC, Mrs Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, said at the Commercial Bid Conference for the Nigeria Licensing Round, themed “Expanding Opportunities: Right Play, Right Place, Right Time”, that the assets on offer have significant reserve potential. “The assets available in this licensing round have potential to add about 500 million barrels to Nigeria’s reserves, increasing our existing reserves of crude oil and condensate—which currently stand at 37.01 billion barrels—and 215.19 trillion cubic feet of gas,” she said. Eyesan said the absence of bids for the 13 frontier blocks was not unexpected. According to her, the assets presented during the 2025 commercial bid had previously been recovered from operators, while the commission would continue assessing other assets for possible inclusion in future licensing exercises. “The reason why we are in the market is because of the blocks that we have recovered from existing operators,” she said. Industry analysts also noted that the licensing round attracted notable investor interest in frontier basins. Some winners The companies that emerged as winners of the 2025 Licensing Round include SSonic Petroleum Limited (PPL 2A29), CFP Pipeline and Flowlines (2A30), Dutchford E&P Limited (2A32), Attabanson Global Company Limited (2A33 and PPL 901), Rosem Energy Limited (2A38), and Pivot-GIS Limited (2A39). The others include Network E&P (2A40), Asharami (2A41), LexOil (2A42), BVOF (2A43), GupscoEnergy Limited (2A44 and 2A51), Saratoga (2A45), Volante (2A46), Concept-Reel Petroleum Services Limited (2A47 and 2A55), Clinton Oil Field (2A48 and 2A62), Nuway Oaklane Limited (2A49), Ramec (2A50), Italia (2A53), Blueridge E&P (2A54), Up Energies Limited (2A56), and AYM Shafa (2A57). There are also Blackrock Holdings Limited (2A58), Funtay Integrated Business Limited (2A59), Riparian Development and Production Limited (2A60), Nikstallis (2A61 and PPL 900), Stardeep Petroleum (PPL 2010), Dakoda & U Limited (PPL 308 and PPL 800), Southborne Oil and Gas Limited (PPL 902), Lanaka Petroleum (PPL 903), Highban Resources Limited (PPL 700) and Eyre Energy Limited (PPL 801). Views from stakeholders Stakeholders have continued to emphasise the importance of pipeline protection to Nigeria’s oil production ambitions, arguing that safeguarding critical infrastructure remains essential to sustaining output, attracting investment and supporting broader economic growth. Related News Over 1,100 host community projects ongoing in Niger Delta, says NUPRC Oil block bidding: Inside Nigeria’s seven-hour transparency test REAN urges action to accelerate Nigeria’s clean energy transition In a published report, the President-General of the Niger Delta Progressive Alliance, Nse Udoh, argued that pipeline surveillance has helped national institutions move from reactive crisis management to more strategic planning and long-term decision-making. “It is important to clarify the role of pipeline surveillance within the wider energy landscape. Energy security encompasses the full value chain, from exploration and production to refining, distribution, pricing policy, and subsidy frameworks. Pipeline surveillance does not manage these domains,” he said. Udoh, however, maintained that pipeline surveillance plays a critical supporting role by protecting infrastructure that transports petroleum resources. “Its mandate is precise: safeguarding critical infrastructure that transports petroleum resources. Yet this single function has proven foundational. Without secure transportation channels, production targets falter, refining plans collapse, exports decline, and fiscal projections become unreliable,” he added. He further argued that asset protection underpins the efficient operation of the petroleum value chain. “Asset protection, in this context, is not a supporting activity. It is a precondition for economic order. In effect, the pipeline is the hinge on which the entire petroleum value chain turns. When that hinge is weak, every other link in the chain carries strain. When it is secure, the entire system gains coherence,” he wrote. According to him, sustained monitoring and rapid-response measures have contributed to fewer pipeline breaches and incidents of illegal tapping, while improvements in production have helped strengthen Nigeria’s position in the international oil market. Udoh also argued that greater certainty in crude oil transportation supports planning across the petroleum value chain. “Economic stability follows predictability. When crude flows are secure, refineries can plan feedstock intake with assurance. Export commitments can be met without fear of sudden shortfalls. Gas-to-power projects can operate without recurrent shutdown risks. “Investors can assess Nigeria’s petroleum sector with clearer risk profiles. Surveillance therefore does more than stop theft. It reintroduces reliability into national energy planning. And reliability is the bedrock upon which sustainable economic growth is built. “With predictable flows, national budgeting becomes more credible, infrastructure planning becomes more precise, and long-term contracts become easier to negotiate. Predictability is the silent currency of modern economies, and pipeline surveillance has begun restoring it,” he stated. He added that improved production accountability has supported export earnings, strengthened foreign exchange inflows and enhanced fiscal capacity, while helping national oil company operations become more efficient through lower losses and improved operational continuity. According to Udoh, more stable revenues also improve government planning by creating greater fiscal certainty and supporting investment in infrastructure, social services and economic diversification. Traditional rulers and community leaders in the Niger Delta have also called for continued support for Tantita Security Services Limited following a vote of confidence passed on the company by the National Assembly. The leaders said the company’s involvement in protecting oil and gas pipelines had coincided with improvements in security across some oil-producing communities, while also creating employment opportunities for young people. Commenting on the development, the President-General of the Isoko Development Union, Christopher Akpotu, commended the joint committee of the Senate and House of Representatives for dismissing petitions filed against the company. He described the decision as beneficial to the Niger Delta and urged stakeholders to focus on expanding opportunities in the oil and gas sector rather than internal disputes. “That is the right way to go,” he said. “There are many opportunities in the oil and gas sector. We should focus on how to derive more benefits rather than fighting over what has already been allocated.” Akpotu cautioned that prolonged disagreements among host communities could create opportunities for outsiders to benefit at their expense. “At the end of the day, if we continue fighting, we give room to those who have no stake in our communities to take what rightfully belongs to us,” he added. While acknowledging concerns about the distribution of benefits, he maintained that the surveillance contract had positively affected many communities. “The truth is that many communities and youths have benefited from the surveillance contract. It may not be evenly distributed, but the impact is evident,” he said. He also urged Tantita to broaden engagement with traditional rulers, youths and community leaders to promote fairness and strengthen long-term cooperation. Similarly, the President-General of the Ughelli Descendants Union, Sam Akpemegi, said security had improved since the company began operations, noting that both physical surveillance and intelligence-driven strategies had been deployed. “They have done very well and improved security since they began operations,” he said, adding that the company’s activities now extend across many communities. Akpemegi added that the company’s presence had benefited both traditional institutions and local residents, while calling for continued support for its operations. In the same vein, the Odiologbo of Ofagbe Kingdom, Ogaga Ikpoku, backed the National Assembly’s decision, describing it as timely and beneficial to peace and stability in the region. Stakeholders also argued that improved protection of oil assets has produced environmental and social benefits in parts of the Niger Delta. They noted that illegal refining and pipeline sabotage had previously polluted waterways, degraded farmlands and exposed communities to environmental and security risks, adding that sustained surveillance efforts against illegal refining sites and repeated pipeline breaches have supported ongoing environmental recovery. “We are in the age of energy transition. NUPRC’s operation in this exercise is good for the economy. It will boost foreign reserves, firm up the naira and macroeconomic environment while deepening foreign capital inflows to the domestic economy,” he said. Yusuf added that stronger protection of oil and gas infrastructure could encourage additional investment in the sector. “The new momentum generated will help build capacity to increase the level of production in the oil and gas industry,” he added.
