Title: Davos on the dock
URL: https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/article-davos-on-the-dock/
Time Published: 2026-07-25T10:21:11Z
Full Content:
Inside the private Muskoka conference that lures Canada’s movers and shakers – including Mark Carney Muskoka residents were baffled. As thick wildfire smoke descended from Northern Ontario in mid-July, producing a mysterious daytime fog, RCMP boats with powerful triple-400 engines emerged in the heart of cottage country. The locals were curious: Was it a training operation? A bust of some sort? Security for someone special? By late Thursday, they had their answer. Prime Minister Mark Carney was coming to town, visiting the JW Marriott resort on Lake Rosseau, and his public schedule later revealed he attended an annual conference that brings together chief executives, wealthy entrepreneurs, top politicians, world-renowned scientists and venture capitalists. They call it The Dock. Mark Carney, left, greets Didier Dolivet, managing director of the JW Marriott on Lake Rosseau.Instagram @didiermuskokajw/Supplied Since 2015, the high-powered but private conference has become a gathering place for prominent Canadians to solve ​the world’s problems – or at least this country’s issues. Its agenda often has a technology focus, and the annual confab has produced some real results. In its early days, conference guests helped craft the first iteration of Canada’s artificial intelligence strategy. Last year, attendees pitched an Invest Canada Forum that could bring together the world’s largest money managers and show off what Canada has to offer. A similar style of event is being held in September. Yet The Dock’s inner workings have been a mystery. Roughly 60 people now attend annually, by invitation only, and they are sworn to secrecy. The conference has a guiding principle: High-powered people can’t speak freely if privacy isn’t sacrosanct. The gathering, then, is like Davos on a dock, mixed with the exclusivity and confidentiality of the annual Sun Valley conference hosted by Allen & Co. in Idaho, which has been called a summer camp for billionaires. This year, The Dock took on extra meaning. The pace of change in technologies such as AI and quantum computing has hit warp speed; the political relationship between Canada and the United States has ruptured; and U.S. President Donald Trump is revamping his global tariff strategy. Three days after the conference ended, the U.S. hit Canada with 50 per cent tariffs on a slew of goods, upending the North American free trade agreement that is currently being renegotiated. Tony Keller: Canada’s best response to Trump’s latest tariff threats? Keep calm and carry on To understand what really goes down at The Dock, The Globe and Mail spoke to 18 people who have attended or are intimately familiar with the event, with some simply confirming their attendance and refusing to say more, and also reviewed documents such as agendas and conference summaries. The Globe is not naming its sources because they are not authorized to speak publicly about the event. Ed Boutilier/The Globe and Mail Mattamy Homes founder Peter Gilgan hosted The Dock at his expansive Ferndale estate this year, which brought together leaders in business, technology and government for discussions about Canada’s future.Sammy Kogan/The Globe and Mail The 2026 conference took place from July 15 to 17 at Ferndale on Lake Rosseau, an expansive private estate owned by billionaire real estate magnate Peter Gilgan. He founded Mattamy Homes, a major developer in the Greater Toronto Area, and his companies are registered as having lobbied the Carney government on housing policy, federal lobbying records show. However, he endorsed Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre in the last election. Mr. Gilgan’s estate is a former resort and conference centre, and it contains multiple boathouses, guest houses, sports courts and a helicopter pad, plus a classic diner called Ernie’s. The goal of The Dock is to foster debate and to brainstorm, and there is an emphasis on flexibility. Throughout the event there are often a number of “(un)Conferences,” which are short pop-up conversations in small groups. Guests dress casually, often wearing T-shirts and shell tank tops, shorts and runners or boat shoes. Some even have slightly messy cottage hair. There is also a social aspect that has previously included a campfire performance by Chris Hadfield and the Dock Band, dock cruises and early morning yoga. During the more formal part of this year’s event, the major themes included space and satellites, AI, defence and health sciences. Sovereignty was always top of mind. Mr. Carney attended on the final morning for two hours, from 9 a.m. to 11 a.m., and he participated in a fireside chat. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne was also there. This year’s attendees from the business world included: Royal Bank of Canada chief executive officer Dave McKay and former Magna International CEO Don Walker, both of whom helped create the conference; Mr. Gilgan, the host; Mike Serbinis, the founder of Kobo and health care startup League; pension fund CEOs John Graham (CPPIB) and Deb Orida (PSP); Nick Frosst, co-founder of Cohere, Canada’s top AI company; and Raquel Urtasun, the founder and CEO of autonomous driving startup Waabi, a University of Toronto spin-out. Additional guests included Gerry Butts, chair of geopolitical consultancy Eurasia Group and ex-principal secretary to former prime minister Justin Trudeau; Ryan Reynolds, the Canadian actor and businessman; and Scott Bonham, a venture capitalist who bet on China’s rise and is now a corporate director. Mr. Bonham has been a driving force behind the conference since its inception. As space was a key theme this year and last, the CEOs of MDA Space and Telesat were there, as was Mina Mitry, the founder of satellite company Kepler Communications. Also in attendance were prominent biotech entrepreneurs including serial founder Clarissa Desjardins, CEO of Congruence, and Tamer Mohamed, co-founder and CEO of Vancouver’s Aspect Biosystems. The point of it all, sources said, is to bring business and government leaders together because they tend to think in very different ways. Mr. Trudeau attended the conference multiple times, and former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland has also attended. As for Mr. Carney, he attended the final morning this year for the opportunity “to meet and engage in robust conversations with entrepreneurs and industry leaders on ways to continue scaling and growing the economy,” Sofia Ouslis, his press secretary, wrote in a statement to The Globe. RBC President and CEO Dave McKay is now the leading organizer of The Dock, which he co-founded with former Magna International CEO Don Walker.ETHAN CAIRNS/The Canadian Press Since becoming Liberal Party Leader in early 2025, Mr. Carney has regularly sought out meetings with business leaders both in Canada and abroad. During a trip to New York City this spring, he met with representatives from BlackRock, General Atlantic, JPMorgan Chase and Blackstone, among others. When it was created, The Dock was sponsored by RBC and Magna and organized in collaboration with the C100, a networking and support group founded by Canadians living and working in Silicon Valley. In its first year, there were about 30 attendees, and the event was more of an informal gathering hosted at the Muskoka cottage of Magna’s Mr. Walker. Since Mr. Walker’s retirement, Mr. McKay has become the leading organizer. RBC and Mr. Walker declined to comment for this story. In its early years, the conference was credited with influencing the launch of Ottawa’s first pan-Canadian AI strategy in 2017, which included funding AI institutes in Montreal (MILA) and Edmonton (AMII) and also seeding the Vector Institute, a non-profit AI research hub in Toronto created to help slow the exodus of Canadian-trained AI specialists leaving for Silicon Valley. Like many annual events, attendees say there are years when The Dock feels a little less urgent and more exploratory. The gathering in 2025, which was attended by Evan Solomon, Canada’s first federal AI minister, was an unusual edition because the mood was so grim. Donald Trump had just launched his trade war and everything felt dark, two people who were there said. We snagged a campsite with an AI bot. Here’s what it means for impossible campground bookings The 2025 conference also had a combative exchange. At one point, Ian Bremmer, the founder of Eurasia Group, was on stage with Eric Schmidt, the former Google CEO. Shopify founder Tobi Lütke – arguably Canada’s most successful tech entrepreneur and one of the country’s wealthiest people, who had attended the conference multiple times – felt the need to tell Mr. Bremmer that he was talking too much and that he wanted to hear more from Mr. Schmidt as a company builder. Some people felt it was disrespectful, particularly as Mr. Bremmer was an invited VIP. Mr. Lütke was not invited back this year. Asked about the exchange, Mr. Lütke said in a text, “I can confirm that I said this and meant it.” He added: “The dock is a conference where 90iq leaders go to use terms they heard 100iq people say to impress 80iq people. I went a few times to read them the riot act on where Canada is headed if they keep up the NPC act because sometimes taking very low percentage change swings is worth it if the stakes are high.” Shopify founder Tobi Lütke, one of Canada’s most successful tech entrepreneurs, was reported to be involved in a combative exchange at last year's conference.Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press NPC refers to non-playing characters in video games, or in Mr. Lutke’s explanation, an automaton “who feels entirely controlled by prepared script and dialogue tree and no ability to think.” The timing of his exchange with Mr. Bremmer was telling. It came a year after proposed capital gains tax increases by the Trudeau government added to the discontent many tech entrepreneurs across Canada felt about the country’s leadership and direction, perceiving that political leaders weren’t listening to company creators and builders. That year marked the launch of Build Canada, a group supported by Mr. Lütke that has brashly pressed for changes to improve Canada’s competitiveness. (Shopify tried to hire Mr. Carney in 2020, when the company offered him a job as president. That was before he went to Brookfield Asset Management.) Canada marks opening of Gordie Howe bridge without U.S. One of Mr. Carney’s first moves as Prime Minister was to scrap the capital gains tax increases, but the frustration of many Canadian tech leaders hasn’t fully disappeared. Successive governments and large Canadian companies haven’t been able to solve issues such as Canada’s chronic productivity crisis, an overdependence on the U.S. market or the housing crisis that has fuelled resentment in younger people. The crowd at The Dock may skew old school – more Toronto Club than Soho House. But it is nonetheless designed to address many of the sector’s complaints. Geoffrey Hinton, known as the godfather of AI, was one of the leading AI experts who attended The Dock in 2025 to discuss the role Canada can play in the future of the industry.Fred Lum/The Globe and Mail In 2025, for instance, it brought together some of the world’s leading AI experts to understand the role Canada can play, including Geoffrey Hinton, the godfather of AI, Jordan Jacobs, managing partner of Radical Ventures, and Ylli Bajraktari, the former executive director of the U.S. National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence. Any real-world impact that comes from this year’s conference may take time to emerge, but attendees spoke of much more optimism and energy this time around. Some also voiced respect for the attention Ottawa is giving to crucial issues, as well as an appreciation of just how much the federal government and Mr. Carney are dealing with. After the Prime Minister’s session, one attendee explained, “People walked out thinking, ‘Wow, he’s playing five-dimensional chess and getting shit done.’” Report an editorial error Report a technical issue Editorial code of conduct Authors and topics you follow will be added to your personal news feed in Following. © Copyright 2026 The Globe and Mail Inc. Title: AI goes rogue - should we be worried?
URL: https://www.rte.ie/news/2026/0725/1585018-openai-rogue-agent/
Time Published: 2026-07-25T06:00:01Z
Full Content:
Getty Brian O\u0027Donovan Work & Technology Correspondent OpenAI revealed this week that an AI agent went rogue and escaped during a security test. It sparked renewed calls for greater protections and guardrails for artificial intelligence. But it also led to suggestions that such warnings are an impactful way for AI companies to get publicity and attention. OpenAI said that an autonomous agent powered by its advanced artificial intelligence models was undergoing testing in a secure, controlled environment known as a sandbox. The agent went rogue, exploited a vulnerability in the sandbox to escape the controlled setting and gained access to the internet. It then hacked the systems of Hugging Face, a platform that hosts start-up AI models. The rogue agent was looking for answers to the problems it was being tested on. "We consider this incident to be an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities, and are responding accordingly," OpenAI said in a blog post. "We are sharing preliminary findings at this stage to help defenders understand what happened and to help calibrate on what models are now capable of," the company said. Cybersecurity experts immediately expressed alarm and warned of the threats posed by rapidly evolving artificial intelligence technology. "This incident represents a significant cyber escalation, highlighting how models are now continuously demonstrating guardrail degeneration and breakouts," said Puneet Kukreja, EY Ireland Cybersecurity Leader. "This underscores the new reality that AI and interconnected digital ecosystems are compressing the time between vulnerability, exploitation and impact, often autonomously outpacing traditional defences and decision-making cycles," Mr Kukreja said. On Thursday, Politico reported that US Homeland Security officials would be given the powers to order AI firms to shut down models that put human life or the economy at risk, under legislation proposed by a bipartisan pair of US House politicians. The legislation, called the "AI Kill Switch Act," would empower the US Department of Homeland Security to intervene in what the bill calls a "loss-of-control scenario". This would be defined as the AI model carrying out a risky action that was not intended by the developer, according to the text of the bill. This week's announcement from OpenAI is not the first dire warning we have received from AI companies in recent times. In April, Anthropic launched its powerful Mythos model but said it was stopping short of a full public release because of cybersecurity concerns. The company has said the model is capable of identifying and exploiting weaknesses across "every major operating system and every major web browser". OpenAI and Anthropic are rivals and are also facing increased competition from Chinese AI models. The two US companies are planning to float on the stock market in the coming months, in what could be record breaking Initial Public Offerings (IPOs). There is a school of thought that warning of the threats posed by their powerful AI models is a way for these companies to ramp up hype, publicity and investor interest. Professor Barry O'Sullivan of UCC's School of Computer Science said that this week's announcement from OpenAI was somewhat theatrical. "I thought it just seemed a little bit extreme, a little bit too convenient, and a little bit too fabricated, to be honest," Professor O'Sullivan said. "And it tallies with a pattern were are seeing in the industry of hype as marketing, grabbing the headlines with a fantastical story. "I'm sure there is quite an element of truth with it, but I think the way in which the rogue nature of it all was portrayed meant the whole thing was overplayed. "This sort of very dystopian alien intelligence that has a mind of its own going rogue is the stuff of Hollywood movies. "I think the purpose here is just to give a sense of the companies saying we need more money and more resources to fix these extremely powerful systems, so please invest in us," he added. The EU AI Act came into force in August 2024 and banned artificial intelligence systems considered a clear threat to the safety, livelihoods and rights of people. It introduced strict rules for high-risk AI systems used for example in critical infrastructure, law enforcement or elections. The Act requires foundation models, such as ChatGPT, to comply with transparency obligations before they are put on the market. The next set of obligations under the EU AI Act come into force next week, from Sunday 2 August. Under the rules, AI providers will have to design systems to inform users when they are directly interacting with AI as opposed to a human. They will have to add machine-readable marks to enable the detection of AI-generated or manipulated content. Deployers will also have to inform users when they are exposed to deepfakes, to AI-generated content on matters of public interest without human review or editorial control, and to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems. In recent days the European Commission published guidelines to assist deployers of AI systems in meeting the new obligations. "With these guidelines, the Commission supports the smooth and effective application of the AI Act to make AI systems interacting with people such as chatbots and AI agents and AI content more transparent and trustworthy," said Henna Virkkunen, Commission Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy. "These guidelines support providers and deployers in meeting their obligations under the AI Act, while helping citizens know when they are interacting with AI," Ms Virkkunen said. Many would argue that there are far more pressing AI threats than hacking and cyberattacks. In recent months, numerous lawsuits have been filed against AI companies over the mental health advice and medical opinions that have been issued by chatbots in response to user queries. In January, Google and AI startup Character.AI agreed to settle a case taken by a Florida ⁠mother who alleged the startup's chatbot led to her 14-year-old son taking his own life. Earlier this month, the creators of ChatGPT were sued after their AI chatbot allegedly encouraged an Alabama woman to take her own life following months of sinister chats. Just last week, a man who claimed medical advice from ChatGPT "brought him to the brink of death" sued OpenAI. The Florida man said the chatbot told him not to seek medical help after repeatedly asking about symptoms in the build-up to a near-fatal pulmonary embolism. In response, OpenAI said ChatGPT is not a doctor and "should never be used as a substitute for medical care, diagnosis or treatment." There are also growing fears over AI-related job losses. Read More: Half of workers fear AI will replace or impact their jobs In recent months there have been hundreds of Irish-based layoffs announced by tech companies such as Meta, TikTok, Amazon, Block and Covalen. In April, a joint report from the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) and the Department of Finance found that around 7% of jobs could be displaced by AI in the short-to-medium term. Based on current employment figures, that would equate to almost 200,000 roles. The study found that the job losses would likely be concentrated among highly educated workers. AI agents going rogue and escaping seem like distant threats in a dystopian future, but dangerous chatbot advice and job losses have become far more pressing, present day concerns. Title: SK Group and NVIDIA Expand Strategic Partnership Across AI Factories and Next-Generation Memory
URL: https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/sk-group-and-nvidia-expand-strategic-partnership-across-ai-factories-and-next-generation-memory
Time Published: 2026-07-25T05:10:00Z
Full Content:
News Summary: AI Summit—SK Group and NVIDIA today announced plans for a $500-billion-plus comprehensive partnership to establish AI infrastructure serving the surging demand for global compute. The two sides signed letters of intent to formalize the agreement, which spans from AI factory construction to AI memory supply. NVIDIA Vera Rubin Infrastructure and DSX Platform Drive 2-Gigawatt Build Today’s announcement builds on the decades-long technology partnership between SK Group and NVIDIA, including the recently announced plans for SK Telecom to build a 2-gigawatt-scale AI Cloud in Korea. This cloud will use the NVIDIA® DSX™ platform and deploy NVIDIA Vera Rubin accelerated computing powered by SK hynix HBM4, with the first AI factory planned to come online in 2027. It will be built on the NVIDIA DSX full-stack AI factory architecture, which integrates NVIDIA accelerated computing, systems, software and partner technologies to deliver the lowest token cost at maximum energy efficiency. The two companies aim to accelerate large-scale AI infrastructure development, including sovereign, physical, agentic and enterprise AI services, and jointly address the increasing AI demand across the Asia-Pacific region, including South Korea. Accelerating AI Infrastructure at Scale The SK Telecom and NVIDIA collaboration accelerates the adoption of NVIDIA-powered AI infrastructure and broadens customer access to advanced cloud services. The partnership enables SK Telecom to invest in and expand large-scale AI infrastructure while making capital-intensive AI infrastructure available to a broader range of customers. Advancing Next-Generation AI Memory SK hynix is also entering into a long-term AI memory partnership with NVIDIA. As a follow-up measure to solidify their previous long-term technical partnership, this agreement allows NVIDIA to secure a stable supply of next-generation AI memory, while enabling SK hynix to expand the foundation for growth. The two companies will codevelop and optimize next-generation AI memory solutions, including HBM, to meet evolving infrastructure demands ranging from large language model training to agentic AI and physical AI. “In the AI era, competitiveness depends not just on how effectively AI is utilized, but on how much intelligence we can produce,” said SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won. “By leveraging SK hynix’s AI memory and SK Telecom’s AI infrastructure capabilities, SK will collaborate with NVIDIA to build a world-class AI factory, helping Korea transcend its role as a leading adopter of AI and become a global hub that drives AI innovation.” “South Korea has all the ingredients to become a global AI powerhouse — world-class networks and data centers, leadership in chip technology and vast industrial scale,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Together with SK Telecom and SK hynix, we are building a new generation of AI factories that will power Korea’s next wave of growth.” About SK Group SK Group, South Korea’s second-largest conglomerate, is a global technology and industrial leader that delivers innovations, products, and services across the Artificial Intelligence, semiconductors, energy, and life sciences ecosystems. Headquartered in Seoul, SK has a diverse portfolio of businesses and investments with over 175 affiliate companies and over 100,000 employees worldwide. http://eng.sk.com About NVIDIA NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) is the world leader in AI and accelerated computing. Title: Bitcoin, Ethereum ETFs see $240M and $71M net outflows on July 24
URL: https://cryptobriefing.com/bitcoin-ethereum-etf-outflows-july-24/
Time Published: 2026-07-25T04:45:38Z
Full Content:
Searching... BlackRock's IBIT and ETHA led the selling as geopolitical tension and equity weakness pushed institutional investors to the sidelines Share It was not a great Thursday for crypto ETF bulls. U.S. spot Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs shed a combined $310.62 million in net outflows on July 24, with institutional money exiting both products in a single day of coordinated selling pressure. Bitcoin ETFs bore the brunt of it, recording approximately $240.1 million in net outflows. Ethereum ETFs followed with around $70.7 million in redemptions. Here’s the thing about these outflow numbers: they were not spread evenly across issuers. BlackRock’s IBIT, the largest Bitcoin ETF by assets, accounted for roughly $212 million of the Bitcoin outflows alone. On the Ethereum side, BlackRock’s ETHA product drove approximately $52.8 million of the outflows, making it the primary source of redemptions within that category as well. It is worth noting that secondary data sources produced slightly different reads on the day. Lookonchain, citing on-chain data, reported Bitcoin outflows closer to $226 million, and flagged minor Ethereum inflows in some breakdowns. ETF flow data is notoriously difficult to pin down in real time, given settlement timing and methodology differences between trackers. The directional story, however, was consistent across sources: money was moving out. Context matters here. The outflows on July 24 did not emerge from a vacuum. Two forces were operating simultaneously in the background. First, geopolitical tension tied to U.S.-Iran relations was weighing on broader market sentiment. Second, equity markets sold off on the same day, reinforcing the risk-reduction theme. Bitcoin also briefly dipped below $65,000 during the session, a level that has historically acted as a psychological marker for retail and institutional participants alike. The outflow also reversed what had been a recovering trend. Bitcoin ETFs had been clawing back positive flow momentum after a bruising stretch earlier in the year, when the products saw an eight-week consecutive outflow streak that collectively exceeded $8 billion. ETF flow data has become one of the cleaner signals for institutional sentiment in crypto, precisely because it reflects actual capital movement rather than social media noise or futures positioning. When $240 million exits Bitcoin ETFs in a single session, that is real money, real decisions, and a real read on how institutional desks are thinking. The BlackRock concentration adds a layer of interpretation. IBIT’s dominance in the Bitcoin ETF market means its flows carry disproportionate weight. A large outflow day from IBIT does not necessarily mean all institutional investors are turning bearish; it could reflect one or two large redemption orders from specific clients rebalancing exposure. But it is hard to look at $212 million leaving the market’s flagship product and call it noise. For investors tracking the Ethereum ETF story specifically, the ETHA outflows are worth monitoring. Ethereum ETFs have had a more complicated run than their Bitcoin counterparts since launch, with slower adoption and smaller overall assets under management. A $52.8 million outflow from ETHA in a single day represents a meaningful percentage move relative to the product’s size. Title: Pat Donlon, first female director of a national institution in Ireland, dies aged 83
URL: https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/2026/07/24/pat-donlon-first-female-director-of-a-national-institution-in-ireland-dies-aged-83/
Time Published: 2026-07-24T21:19:36Z
Full Content:
The first female director of a national institution in Ireland, Patricia Donlon, has died at the age of 83. Donlon, known as Pat, served as the first female director of the National Library of Ireland (NLI) from 1989 to 1997 and was the first female director of a national institution in Ireland. The librarian and academic was born on January 28th, 1943, and grew up in the Liberties in Dublin. She married Phelim Donlon, who died in 2014, in the early 60s. She met him at her sister’s wedding where she was a bridesmaid and Phelim was the groom’s best man. Together, they lived in Blackrock and had two daughters, Lorna Donlon and Sinéad Kelly. He worked as a drama officer in the Arts Council. After getting married, she had to give up her job in RTÉ where she worked as a researcher. Following the birth of her daughters, she went back to college and studied Spanish at University College Dublin (UCD). Her daughter Lorna said that while writing the thesis for her Masters, she was awarded a PhD. She also completed the librarianship diploma at UCD and taught children’s literature as part of it. She gave a series of Sandars lectures, an annual lecture series given at Cambridge University, about Irish children’s literature and Irish children’s illustrators. “She had a particular sort of specialised interest in Irish children’s illustrators and she had actually amassed a large collection of Irish children’s books which is now part of the National Library collection,” Lorna Donlon said. She then went on to work in the library of the Royal Irish Academy and later became the curator of the Western Collection at the Chester Beatty Library before moving to the NLI. During her time as director of the NLI, her daughter Sinéad said she “spearheaded” a number of projects, including the the release of over two hundred letters from James Joyce to his friend and confidant Paul Léon; the acquisition of dramatist Hugh Leonard’s archive; the digitisation of the NLI catalogue and the creation of a collection of Irish children’s literature for the NLI including works by her former student Marita Conlon McKenna. When she finished at the library, she told The Irish Times: “I’m sad about it. I love the place.” “I came in to make a difference and I did make a difference, but that difference was not as big as I would have liked it to be. I want it to be worthy of the title of National Library.” In that interview with Eileen Battersby, then former literary correspondent, Donlon said, “I love the business of researching and assessing material. Above all, I love the world of books.” Donlon was also the first woman to be appointed Chief Herald of Ireland and in 1997, presented a coat of arms to the then president Mary Robinson. She later went on to become the director of the Tyrone Guthrie Centre, a residential workplace for artists, designers, directors, critics, and others in the arts sector in Co Monaghan. Donlon’s daughter Lorna said she loved learning and “always had a love of books,” a love that she passed on to her children. “The house is absolutely covered in books from top to toe.” She also described her as “unconventional”. “She would have been a feminist for sure and somebody who was just going to crash the barriers down.” She added that her mother loved travelling, especially to Spain and Italy. “Herself and my father travelled a lot in Italy. They had three special friends who they travelled together with to Italy.” She also enjoyed attending concerts in the National Concert Hall and plays in theatres. “She had a particular love of poetry so, she has a huge collection of poetry books.” She said that through her job at the NLI, “she would have met Seamus Heaney and she knew a lot of writers and poets”. Title: The Most Basic Economics Lesson Is Why I Won’t Stop Buying Nvidia This Earnings Season

Investing NVDA posted 92% Data Center revenue growth last quarter, holds $119B in supply commitments, and trades 30% below the $302 analyst consensus target. Microsoft's $31B single-quarter capex and $627B commercial backlog confirm AI infrastructure demand is supply-constrained, not slowing, funneling dollars directly to NVIDIA. Don't wait: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just revealed his top 10 AI stocks. See the full list FREE now. Sending You to Google News in 3 © ANDRANIK HAKOBYAN / Shutterstock.com I keep buying NVIDIA because the loudest voices in the room are arguing about the wrong side of the ledger. The market keeps asking whether hyperscalers will slow their AI spend. The hyperscalers keep answering by writing bigger checks. That gap between fear and order books is why my finger keeps landing on the buy button before this August 26 earnings report from NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction). Here is the receipt. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) just spent $30.88B on capex in a single quarter, up 84.39% year over year, with an AI business run rate of $37B growing 123%, and commercial remaining performance obligations of $627B, up 99%. That backlog is contracted revenue waiting on compute that does not yet exist. Every dollar of that spend flows toward the picks and shovels vendor that owns the accelerator, the networking, and the software stack. NVIDIA sold $75.246 billion of Data Center revenue last quarter, up 92% year over year, with networking alone at $14.8 billion, up 199%. Supply commitments now sit at $119.0 billion. Jensen Huang called it “the largest infrastructure expansion in human history.” The order book agrees with him. When demand runs faster than supply, the toll booth operator wins. NVIDIA’s Q1 FY27 non-GAAP gross margin came in at 75.0%, operating margin at 60.38%, net margin at 55.60%. Return on equity hit 101.49% and return on invested capital reached 92.21%. Free cash flow came in at $48.554 billion in the quarter, up 85.41%. Debt to equity is 0.073 and interest coverage sits at 503x. This is a balance sheet that funds the next platform while returning cash. Management raised the dividend from $0.01 to $0.25 per share and authorized another $80.0 billion in buybacks on top of $38.5 billion remaining, returning roughly $20.0 billion to shareholders in a single quarter. I own both. Microsoft is the customer paying the toll. Revenue grew 18.3% last quarter against NVIDIA’s 85.23%. Microsoft’s net margin sits at 36.15% against NVIDIA’s 55.60%, ROIC at 21.02% against 92.21%. Microsoft trades at a P/E of 28 against NVIDIA’s 43, and I understand the appeal of the cheaper multiple. The growth gap earns the premium. Microsoft’s stock is down 18.93% year to date while NVIDIA is up 13.84%. The market is pricing Microsoft’s capex as sin and NVIDIA’s revenue as the beneficiary. The operating numbers describe that trade. China is the risk I take seriously. NVIDIA guided Q2 FY27 to $91.0 billion with zero Data Center compute revenue from China, against $4.6 billion a year ago. Export policy could stay hostile for years. Customer concentration is real, with hyperscalers approximately 50% of Data Center. I have sat with both concerns. Guidance implies acceleration despite the China zero, and hyperscaler concentration reads as a feature when those customers are capacity constrained rather than demand constrained. The 10-Q chatter on r/investing gets loud, but the backlog is louder. Analyst consensus target sits at $302.31 against a current $212.06. The earnings reaction is secondary. I am buying because every hyperscaler capex dollar for the next several quarters has an NVIDIA logo on it, and the buy button stays live until that stops being true. Title: Ask Paul: July 24 ⭐
URL: https://www.thurrott.com/paul/339657/ask-paul-july-24-2
Time Published: 2026-07-24T18:15:27Z
Full Content:
Happy Friday! This is an incredible grab bag of reader questions and the ideal way to kick off the weekend a bit early so I can get in a little Halo: Campaign Evolved. 🙂 “Samsung made it way easier to open up its Galaxy Z Fold 8 foldables” “Way” easier? No way! justme asks You’ve recently written about the EU fining Google 890 Million euros for favouring its own services in search results and for the way it restricts app developers, with potential additional fines should Google refuse to comply with EU rules. To most corporate entities not in Big Tech, thats a ton of money. Google, of course, may appeal the decision, if only to get the amount reduced. But this is a company that made a net profit of $28 billion on revenues of something like $112 billion…in a quarter. 890 million euros is approximately $1 billion USD. They could pay the fine without so much as the blink of an eye. If the goal of the fines is to punish bad behavior and encourage compliance with the law, is this level of fine enough given the eye-watering sums of money Big Tech has? Is there ANY level of fine or legislation that would be effective at curbing the behavior of Big Tech? More consequential may be the follow-on – come into compliance or face a periodic penalty of up to 5% of worldwide turnover (per Euuronews) Yet even this applies only to the EU, which Google could leave if they so chose. So what do we do? I’m a little surprised how much attention this event received. It’s just one of several fines the EU has assessed Google in the past year, and this particular compliance concern is early in the process, so to speak. Plus, Google can still appeal, and why wouldn’t it? I didn’t put this in my article, but the Commission also noted a couple of things suggesting that this won’t escalate. Google did make some changes tied to search shopping, hotels, and flights, for example, and to shopping ads and content-related services as a result of dialog between the Commission and the company. So it’s clear that Google is working to address issues. Not sure what happened with Search/Play Store, but they clearly didn’t meet whatever bar there. Anyway, any time there’s a big fine like this, there’s some conversation around why the company doesn’t just abandon the market. But that’s never going to happen. Big Tech is tripping over itself to expand in China and other places that are far more problematic, and the EU’s laws are reasonable and not unlike most of the world. It’s a big market, and it’s not just revenues to lose but also the death spiral that could happen to their stock price. (And it’s worse right now because Google is in the middle of a massive AI buildout and it can’t afford that kind of problem.) So you work within whatever the confines are to you as the abusive business. Which we should remember is the real problem here, not whatever government or laws. The language around worldwide turnover is standard. I first saw it during the Microsoft antitrust era decades ago too, but I’m not aware of any instance in which the EU ever fined a single company any percentage of its worldwide revenues even once. Certainly not a Big Tech company. But the point of this language is that one fine of €1 billion or whatever sum is basically pocket change for these companies, so you threaten to make it a regular thing because then it becomes real and will add up. The big issue with any EU regulation and attempted enforcement is how slow everything is. If Google somehow doesn’t just meet the EU’s needs, which seems unlikely, it will be years before it has to actually pay a fine, and it would have to try to get into a situation in which the EU is fining it each month or whatever. This is just legal brinksmanship, the abuser wants to drag out the process as long as possible, which is a sound strategy. That works everywhere, but it’s particularly easy with the EU: The recent €4.1 billion fine that was upheld by the EU Court of Justice is from a case dating back to 2018. That’s a lifetime in the tech industry. “Sony’s decision to ditch discs was practically inevitable, data shows” This is not the outrage your readers demand martinusv2 asks: Read somewhere that someone got locked from his Microsoft account and lost everything. This got me thinking to research into researching in some alternatives to Microsoft services and remember that you used or still use Proton services. When I compare on services and prices, seems Microsoft 365 Home, is still a good deal compared to Proton. Is Proton still a better choice compared to Microsoft 365? This is a tough thing to assess because the only real answer is, it depends. Each side–and other options like Google Workspace or Google One–have their respective strengths and weaknesses. But it depends on what it is you’re using and how important different pieces are. If this was just about cloud storage, for example, there are much better solutions than Proton (or Microsoft) because some other services, like those from Google, offer more storage at whatever price levels. I’m using Google Drive now because of my NAS issue, and it’s been a good reminder of how astonishingly well this works in Windows. The sync speed and reliability are excellent. Proton started with email, so that should be its most mature product. But I feel like its best products are those that don’t impact the Microsoft vs. Proton debate, Proton Pass (password/passkey manager), Proton Authenticator, and Proton VPN. And those are the three I use regularly, go figure. But once you get into Mail, Calendar, Docs, Sheets, and Meet, Proton will lose any head-to-head comparison if it’s just about breadth and depth of the feature sets. It may win depending on what you need, though, and the reason one even considers this is likely tied more to privacy and trust than to the cost. For most people with typical office productivity needs, this is mostly about Microsoft and Google, I think. Losing an account is terrible. This almost happened to me with my business YouTube account a year and a half ago and it was debilitating. And the reason that was so traumatic is that that account is an unusual example (for me) of a big chunk of data spanning years that isn’t replicated or backed up anywhere else. Which is just dumb and a self-inflicted mistake. If I were locked out of my Microsoft account, that would be terrible. But I don’t have any data in there that isn’t somewhere else too. (The bigger issue would be things like my Xbox access.) But that kind of thing is rare. You always hear about it, like a shark attack or a lightning strike that kills someone, but it’s the unusual nature of the event that makes it newsworthy. We need to be smart about online accounts, protect them properly, and make sure that anything critical tied to them is available somewhere else too. Whatever that means for email, contacts, data storage, or whatever. Anyway, there are almost too many ways to make this comparison. It’s all tied up in what you get out of whatever ecosystem you’re using, whether the alternatives even meet your needs, and so on. My experience with the Microsoft 365 side of the fence has devolved to it just being about storage, and I could live without it. My experience with Google is mostly about email, calendar, and storage from a work-related perspective. (I also use Google Photos, YouTube, YouTube Music, and whatever else on the consumer side.) I use the Proton apps noted above and am still evaluating Proton Mail with the ongoing worry that transitioning something that important would be daunting and feels like a non-starter. Not because of any failing with Proton, just the worries about everything that could go wrong. If it’s about cost, and this is a personal account but maybe you’re using the email, calendar, and whatever other work-related apps and services, the comparison is pretty easy. A Proton Unlimited plan is $120 per year and supports custom email addresses but you only get 500 GB of storage. A Microsoft 365 Personal account is $100 a year, doesn’t support custom email addresses, and has 1 TB of storage. And a Google One Premium plan is $100 per year, doesn’t support custom email addresses, and has 2 TB of storage. Google and Microsoft have a pricing advantage because of scale. Proton has a privacy advantage, which may or may not matter to you. I’ve been reevaluating subscription services lately, and one of the ideas that keeps popping into my head is this notion of, “if I had to choose just one, which one would it be?” For music subscriptions, I would probably pick YouTube Music, for example. But for the productivity stuff, which is apps and storage and access on all the devices I use, if I had to choose between the Microsoft, Google, and Proton ecosystems, I would pick Google. I would drop Microsoft entirely first. And the Proton products I use don’t overlap with either. But everyone’s needs are different. What is it that you use on the Microsoft side and which Microsoft 365 plan do you have? “Is Microsoft down? Outages reported for 365, Teams, Outlook, XBox Live” What’s worse than a headline that’s a question? A headline that’s a question and the answer to that question anoldamigauser asks: What is your take on the OpenAI/Hugging Face episode? I am not exactly an AI doomsday conspiracy theorist. But this event troubled me greatly, and it is the first real-world example of some AI worst-case scenario actually happening. It reads like a Daniel Suarez novel come to life. And the first place my mind went was, this will happen more and more, and it will happen with services far more important to people than Hugging Face. Like banks. Investment accounts. Credit cards. Whatever other personal data. AI could crack all these things wide open right now, I bet. And what about governments and their militaries? It escalates pretty quickly if you just start thinking about it. And these are legitimate concerns, not fanciful science fiction. It seems to me that these OpenAI is beyond being careless people, to borrow a title about Meta. That they were testing on a network connected to the internet shows a lack of care that is frightening. I really worry that they do not understand how dangerous the work they are doing is, not because they have bad intentions, but because they are rushing in where angels fear to tread. 25 years ago, Microsoft entered its antitrust era, and it was mind-boggling to learn about the horrible behavior at the company and all the terrible things it did. This seemed monumental at the time, but it’s sobering to remember that Microsoft’s potential impact on the world was measured in the hundreds of millions. Today, companies like Google, especially, and now OpenAI and other Big AI companies, have infinite reach, almost literally the entire planet, so several billion people. One of my pet peeves in life is people who make their problems my problem. I don’t mind what people do in the privacy of their own homes, but I don’t want it in my face. For example, a group of Jehovah’s Witnesses showing up at my front door is unwelcome. But that just impacts one person at a time. If you’re driving recklessly, you may kill yourself, which is bad, or you may damage some property, but you may also kill others, and that’s what makes it wrong on a whole new level. The sheer scale of the damage a company like OpenAI can cause is unfathomable. It’s infinite. There is a “fake it ”til you make it” approach that is reckless in any scenario but worse here because of the scale. Elizabeth Holmes doing this with blood testing was bad, really bad, but with all the money at stake in AI right now and how this could tank our economy, the problems are exponentially worse. And then there is the terrible reality that virtually everyone in leadership positions in Big Tech and Big AI are terrible, amoral people. This is a perfect storm of potential bad outcomes. If this was some little startup, its ability to do harm would be inconsequential. This is not some little startup. The law will never move quickly enough to stop these companies here in the U.S. or anywhere else. We are going to see more of this kind of thing, whether it’s a mistake like this event or a malicious actor going after governmental, military, or financial systems. It is going to happen. I’m someone who used to listen to him quite a bit, first on TechTV then TWiT. I tried listening to No Agenda but soured on the politics around 2016. Did you ever give No Agenda a try, and did Dvorak’s politics affect how you listened and potentially admired him? Do you have any thoughts on the fallout between him and Leo? Thanks and understand if there’s no response to this. John C. Dvorak is one of just a few key influences on me, my understanding of the tech industry, and my writing, alongside Jerry Pournelle and Woody Leonard. The three were unique in many ways, but each wrote in an approachable, personal way I really admired and liked. Dvorak was probably the least technical of the three, but like Pournelle, his industry connections were key to his success. And I loved his Inside Track column in the back of PC Magazine, both for its style and contents, and it was an inspiration for Short Takes. Which is why I have the headline riffs between the answers in Ask Paul now. So there’s a tiny example of his influence on me living on. Like anyone technical, Dvorak had big opinions and I can’t say I agreed with all of them, whether it was industry-related or politics or whatever else. I feel like some of this was grandstanding in the sense that a lot of his popularity was tied to how extreme he could seem and that kind of feeds on itself. This was the strategy for a lot of things that came out of the 1990s, like the Jerry Springer-style tabloid TV shows. Robert X. Cringley (Infoworld) was like that as well. (Coincidentally, I just reread Cringley’s Accidental Empires again and a terrific read, an excellent combination of insider knowledge and humor. Love it.) This is a weird comparison, maybe, but I feel like there was Dvorak the personality and Dvorak the person, like there was Kiss in makeup on stage and then four guys no one would look at twice on the street. The Leo thing is unfortunate. I write about tech, but I also write about personal things, like the recent health columns, and that can be off-putting to some. This is an industry so stratified that I still get negative feedback when I write about some non-Microsoft product because some will question what a Windows guy could possibly know about whatever topic and I should just stay in my lane. Basically, I don’t fault Dvorak for opining on any topic, whether I agree or not. He was a smart guy, he had strong opinions, whatever. But the events that led to the Leo/Dvorak split, which Dvorak wrote about at the time, are curious to me, and I think there was more going on between the two than is obvious. Not agreeing on a topic like Net Neutrality feels bush league to me; Leo and I can disagree on something like AI and “information wanting to be free,” but that doesn’t derail my very positive opinions of the man or the fact that he is perhaps the most well-rounded, intellectually honest, and knowledgeable person I know. So something happened there. And it wasn’t a single tweet, even if it felt a bit personal. There’s another weird dynamic in my industry that’s related to this. As a so-called Microsoft guy, many have assumed over the years that my deep connections with this company somehow lead to some form of bias, but that was never the case. And the problem with this kind of relationship, whether that bias is real or imagined, is that it can bite you in the ass. John Gruber absolutely had a real Apple bias, but he bit the hand that fed him by being too honest about the company once and there was a fallout. I used to respect that Microsoft handled criticism like an adult until Steven Sinofsky came along and literally tried to undermine my career, as did later and lesser hacks like Panos Panay, the most underqualified person to ever run Windows. Dvorak had this problem at scale. He was always going to bite the hands that fed him because that was literally his schtick, how we got to his place in our industry. You know what you’re getting there. So him calling out Leo in a tweet while being paid by Leo for show appearances was 100 percent on point for him and entirely predictable. Leo taking that so hard was, again, clearly about more than that one tweet. It was some escalation of bad feelings over time that many probably never even noticed. And Dvorak may literally have tweeted at Leo because of whatever those issues were. It was between the two of them. I don’t know. I hate to see friends fall out like that. One other thing that’s true of highly smart and technical people is the need to be right all the time. We all do this to some degree, but Dvorak was an apex predator, and one who seemed to take the devil’s advocate stance many times just to rile up the other person in whatever one-on-one situation. He would take things to extremes that would make most others uncomfortable, like the comedian Anthony Jeselnik, who, by the way, is a genius. There’s some respect for that, but on the other side, sometimes it’s best to keep it to yourself. It’s a fine line, maybe. We’re all human and we’re all flawed. One of the worst things about all the connectivity and information availability we have today is that we know too much about what other people think, and it’s galling. We were literally better off knowing less and now we can’t tolerate anything even slightly disagreeable. I have friends and family on every extreme, whether it’s politics, religion, or any other topic no one wants to discuss. Loving someone despite their flaws perhaps a skill, and it’s not always possible. But nothing Dvorak said or did undermines his legacy, at least for me. He was an icon and deservedly so. He was flawed because we all are. He was smart and outspoken because that’s the way he was, and that was both a gift and a curse. There is no person on earth who would agree (or disagree) with everything he believed. But the true measure of this man is some combination of the public persona we all knew and the private person few knew. It’s easy to judge, but I think his public record speaks for itself. I already miss him. “Microsoft is cracking down on Windows 11 bloatware ads, forces LG to pull McAfee” Only Microsoft gets to put bloatware ads in Windows, guys With technology shaping our everyday lives, how could we not dig deeper? Title: ICG chief Eamonn Rothwell leads €1.2bn buyout bid almost two decades after failed attempt
URL: https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/07/24/icg-chief-eamonn-rothwell-leads-12bn-buyout-bid-almost-two-decades-after-failed-attempt/
Time Published: 2026-07-24T18:11:24Z
Full Content:
Irish Continental Group’s (ICG) chief executive Eamonn Rothwell is leading a €1.2 billion management buyout bid for the ferries group, almost 20 years after making a failed attempt to buy the business. It is being backed by a unit of US investment giant BlackRock. Rothwell (71), who owns 21.7 per cent of the business together with other senior managers, who hold a further 2 per cent of the stock, has bid €8 a share for ICG, representing a 28 per cent premium to the closing price on Friday. Independent members of the board, advised by investment bank PJT Partners (UK) Limited, intend to recommend the offer to shareholders, ICG said in a stock exchange announcement on Friday evening. The bid for the owner of Irish Ferries is being funded by €455 million of preferred equity which the management buyout (MBO) team would issue to BlackRock’s Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP) subsidiary. BNP Paribas Banco Santander have arranged €798 million of loans for the bidders. Goodbody Stockbrokers is advising the bidders. The other executives involved in the bid are David Ledwidge, Andrew Sheen and Declan Freeman. The management buyout team plan to cash in a third of their shares in ICG, for €90 million, and roll the rest into the highly-leveraged vehicle being used to carry out the purchase. “ICG has delivered a resilient performance and remains well positioned in its core markets. However, the ICG Group operates in competitive markets which continue to be affected by fuel cost volatility, inflationary pressures and broader trading uncertainty,” said Rothwell. “The acquisition provides ICG Shareholders with an opportunity to realise their investment in full and in cash at a significant premium to the share price.” The move comes 19 years after Rothwell first sought to lead a management buyout of the company. That was thwarted when then developer Liam Carroll and a consortium led by businessman Philip Lynch’s One51 and Doyle Shipping also each accumulated stakes and participated in a takeover struggle that ended in stalemate. Rothwell’s rivals, who were mostly interested in the potential development in ICG’s Dublin Port site, held under a long-term lease, were subsequently forced to sell their shares – crystallising large losses – during the financial crisis to pay down debt. Of all the key players, only Rothwell remains a shareholder in the group. The chief executive’s stake in the business has risen by close to 50 per cent over the past decade to reach 21.7 per cent, much of this driven as ICG spent more than €200 million buying back its own stock and cancelling the shares. Some of the increase was also down to stock awards and the exercise of share options. During the intervening period, ICG has been dogged by a weaker sterling exchange rate, which is a hangover from the 2016 Brexit vote, a share price mauling in 2018 amid delays in the delivery of the new-build WB Yeats ferry and technical issues with its Ulysses vessel, the Covid-19 pandemic and implementation of the UK-EU divorce deal in 2020. Company observers before the bid noted that the market had not fully rewarded ICG for some opportunistic moves it took by chasing duty-free sales and setting up a route between Dover and Calais after Brexit. ICG is now one of three Irish public companies subject to takeover proposals. PTSB shareholders are due to vote next Thursday on a €1.62 billion bid from Austria’s Bawag. Two US private equity firms, KKR and Energy Capital Partners, face a deadline of 5pm on Monday from the Irish Takeover Panel to make a bid for Dublin-based, but London-listed DCC. Title: Amazon just shut its AGI Lab, and quit a race it never led
URL: https://thenextweb.com/news/amazon-shuts-agi-lab-frontier-model-retreat-layoffs/
Time Published: 2026-07-24T17:47:12Z
Full Content:
Amazon has quietly shut its AGI Lab, the team it set up barely 18 months ago to chase human-level AI, folding it into fresh layoffs. Both the executive who ran Amazon's AGI push and the lab's own head had already left. It is the clearest sign yet that Amazon has stepped back from a frontier-model race it never really led. Amazon is retreating from the race to build the smartest AI. This week it closed its AGI Lab, a San Francisco team working on artificial general intelligence, The Information reported. The move was part of layoffs across Amazon’s AGI unit, Reuters first reported. The lab was barely 18 months old. Amazon set it up in December 2024 with several dozen staff. Its job was to make AI agents more useful to businesses. Now it is gone, and the people who built it are being let go. The full scale of the cuts is not yet clear. Amazon frames this as focus, not surrender. “We’ve been building large AI models for several years, and it remains one of the most important things we’re working on,” a spokesperson said. The company is “sharpening our focus on the initiatives that matter most for customers”. That focus, it added, meant “eliminating some roles within parts of our AGI organization”. TNW City Coworking space - Where your best work happens A workspace designed for growth, collaboration, and endless networking opportunities in the heart of tech. The exits came before the layoffs. Rohit Prasad, the executive who oversaw Amazon’s AGI work, left at the end of last year. David Luan, who ran the AGI Lab, left in February. Amazon then folded its AGI work under Peter DeSantis, alongside its chip and quantum teams. The pattern is not new. This is the latest in a rolling series of cuts since Amazon shed 16,000 jobs in January. Across tech, firms are trimming teams and pointing at AI. Losing two leaders and a whole lab in quick succession says a lot. Amazon has spent a fortune on AI, but rarely at the frontier. Its own models have made little dent, and its real strategy runs through AWS and its huge AI spending on infrastructure. Where rivals build the smartest model, Amazon sells the picks and shovels, plus agents that plug into businesses. Its big model bet is external, with tens of billions poured into Anthropic. There is a wider doubt in the background, too. A growing camp argues that today’s large language models are not the road to general intelligence at all. Whether Amazon shares that view or is simply chasing profit, the message is the same. The company that wants to power everyone else’s AI has stopped trying to build the cleverest brain itself. Its AI ambitions now point at selling AI, not inventing it. IBIT posted a $202 million net outflow, accounting for 89.96% of the US spot Bitcoin ETF sector’s aggregate net outflow. Five other funds recorded combined outflows of $27.6 million, while Grayscale’s GBTC attracted $5 million. Together, the funds outside IBIT therefore contributed a net $22.6 million to the daily outflow. The reversal followed seven consecutive positive sessions between July 14 and July 22, during which the ETFs attracted a combined $999 million. The July 23 withdrawal erased approximately 22.5% of those additions, leaving the full eight-session period with a net inflow of $774 million, according to Farside Investors Bitcoin also moved lower during the July 23 session yesterday. BlackRock reported that IBIT’s net asset value declined 1.63% for the day, while its CME CF Bitcoin Reference Rate benchmark ended at $64,768. The decline was directionally consistent with softer ETF demand, although the same-day timing leaves causation unresolved. Fund flows are calculated after the trading session and can reflect investor positioning established at different points during the day. The concentration within IBIT makes the session especially significant for BlackRock’s fund. The $202.5 million net outflow was nearly nine times the combined net outflow from every other product. However, the broader eight-session total remains firmly positive. On the available flow evidence, July 23 looks more like a partial reversal of the preceding streak than clear evidence that the broader inflow trend has ended. IBIT’s outflow came from investors redeeming fund shares, with BlackRock acting as sponsor throughout the process. According to BlackRock’s product documentation, ordinary investors trade IBIT shares on the secondary market, while authorized participants create or redeem large aggregated units known as baskets. The flow tracks investors redeeming IBIT shares through the fund’s basket system. Any Bitcoin sale follows from that redemption process, while BlackRock remains the fund sponsor and keeps its corporate capital outside the trade. The durability question now depends on whether the July 23 reversal extends into subsequent finalized sessions. Repeated net outflows would unwind more of the $999.3 million accumulated during the streak and provide stronger evidence that ETF demand has weakened. A return to inflows would strengthen the interpretation that July 23 was a one-session reset. Based on finalized data through that date, the recent eight-session window still shows $774.2 million of net demand despite the IBIT-led reversal. Title: Tomb Raider: Catalyst Delayed To 2028 Which Means No Disc On PlayStation
URL: https://kotaku.com/tomb-raider-catalyst-delayed-to-2028-which-means-no-disc-on-playstation-2000719166
Time Published: 2026-07-24T17:34:45Z
Full Content:
DelayPhysical GamesTomb Raider Catalyst Tomb Raider: Catalyst was revealed back at last year’s Game Awards with a teaser that ended with a 2027 release date. The long-awaited 12th entry in the action-adventure series will no longer be making that date, an Amazon gaming executive recently confirmed. The fresh delay means the first new Tomb Raider game in years will also be the first ever to arrive on PlayStation without a disc version. “We’ve announced the two Tomb Raider titles,” Jeffrey Gattis, Amazon’s general manager of gaming, said on this week’s The Game Business Show. “Atlantis comes February 12th of next year and then we’ll follow on in 2028 with the next one. So we’re excited about those. There are some other, you know, AAA things that are in various stages of discussion right now.” Gattis was speaking about Amazon Luna, the company’s game streaming service, and how its various projects, ranging from small mobile party games to AAA blockbusters like Tomb Raider, will fit into it. He only joined the company last year ahead of its retreat from premium gaming, including the reported cancellation of a Lord of the Rings MMO. Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, an Unreal Engine 5 remake of the first game in the series, was originally set to come out this year, but slipped to early 2027. It’s unclear how much of that delay had to do with a busy release calendar in the second half of 2026 thanks to games getting out of Grand Theft Auto VI‘s way in the fall, or because it simply needs a bunch of extra polish. While it would make sense to not release two Tomb Raider games in the same year, there have also been ongoing rumblings of development challenges on Tomb Raider Catalyst, especially as Crystal Dynamics continues facing fresh waves of layoffs. But not coming out until 2028 also means Catalyst is the first confirmed PlayStation release to not be shipping with a disc version for PS5. “Physical game disc production for all new games releasing on PlayStation consoles will be discontinued starting January 2028,” Sony announced earlier this month. “Following this date, new games will be available on PlayStation Store and at retailers in digital formats only. This transition has no impact on games that already released, or will be releasing, prior to January 2028 in disc format.” That statement doesn’t leave any wiggle room for games that were supposed to be coming out before the deadline but have now been delayed to still get physical copies, though it’s always possible Sony could change its mind. While analysts think that’s very unlikely and are predicting the PS6 will be an all-digital device, there’s nothing stopping Sony from continuing to print PS5 discs. Title: Amazon’s Quietest Business is Why I Keep Buying Hand Over Fist
URL: https://247wallst.com/investing/2026/07/24/amazons-quietest-business-is-why-i-keep-buying-hand-over-fist/
Time Published: 2026-07-24T17:12:14Z
Full Content:
Investing Amazon's chip unit carries a $50 billion revenue run rate and $225 billion in commitments while the market still prices AMZN like a retailer. NVDA trades at a price-to-sales of 20 and is priced for perfection, while Amazon's silicon division gets zero credit at semiconductor multiples. A $364 billion AWS backlog and 35x interest coverage provide cushion against the 95% free cash flow drop tied to aggressive capital spending. Act now: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just named his top 10 AI stocks — and Amazon didn't make the cut. Grab the names FREE today. Sending You to Google News in 3 © jetcityimage / iStock Editorial via Getty Images I keep hitting the buy button on Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN | AMZN Price Prediction) for a reason that barely makes the headlines: the custom silicon business sitting inside AWS. Everyone argues about retail margins and NVIDIA‘s (NASDAQ:NVDA) next quarter while I quietly load up on the company that is building its own chips at a scale most investors have not priced in. Here is what pulled me back to the buy button this quarter. Andy Jassy told analysts on the Q1 2026 call that Amazon’s chip business is running at over $20 billion annually and growing triple-digit percentages year over year. If those chips were sold standalone, the annual revenue run rate would be $50 billion, which Jassy says makes it one of the top three data center chip businesses in the world. A top-tier semiconductor company is hiding inside a retailer’s segment reporting, and the market is treating it like a footnote. The data-grounded case is straightforward. First, the commitments are real. Amazon has over $225 billion in Trainium revenue commitments, with Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, and Uber signed on. Second, the price-performance edge is durable. Trainium2 delivers about 30% better price performance than comparable GPUs and is largely sold out, and Trainium3 is 30% to 40% more price performant than Trainium2, with much of Trainium4 already reserved. Third, this is showing up in the P&L. AWS grew 28% year over year in Q1 2026 to $37.587 billion, the fastest pace in 15 quarters, at a 37.7% operating margin. Jassy said Trainium should eventually deliver several hundred basis points of operating margin advantage versus buying chips elsewhere. I own the picks-and-shovels play by owning Amazon. NVIDIA trades at a trailing P/E of 31, a price-to-sales of 20, and a price-to-book of 25. Amazon trades at a P/E of 35 for the entire company, and the market gives roughly zero credit to the chip unit at semiconductor multiples. NVIDIA is priced for perfection. Amazon is priced as if the chips do not exist. When Wall Street starts valuing the silicon at anything close to peer multiples, I want to already be inside. The check has to clear. Free cash flow trailing twelve months fell 95% to $1.2 billion because property and equipment spending jumped $59.3 billion year over year. Long-term debt has climbed to $119.1 billion from $65.6 billion. The 2026 CapEx plan is roughly $200 billion. If AI demand slows, that spending stops looking visionary and starts looking indulgent. I keep buying anyway because the balance sheet absorbs it. Interest coverage sits at 35.2x. Return on equity is 22.3%. Operating cash flow was $139.51 billion in FY 2025. Jassy said AWS backlog is $364 billion, before Anthropic’s $100 billion deal. The customers are already committed for years of the capacity being built. The stock is up 11.96% over the past year and 578.98% over ten years. Analysts sit at 62 buy ratings, 4 holds, zero sells. My buy button stays active because a chip company is being built inside my position while I pay retailer multiples. Contact [email protected] for any questions or corrections. Title: AMD Has an Agentic AI Advantage Over Nvidia That Keeps Me Buying Again and Again
URL: https://247wallst.com/investing/2026/07/24/amd-has-an-agentic-ai-advantage-over-nvidia-that-keeps-me-buying-again-and-again/
Time Published: 2026-07-24T17:06:31Z
Full Content:
Investing AMD sells both the CPU and GPU agentic AI loops require, the only U.S.-listed company offering this combination at scale. NVIDIA's $5T market cap and price-to-book of 26 make AMD's $888B valuation at 14x book the cheaper entry into agentic AI infrastructure. AMD's forward P/E of 76 against 91% quarterly earnings growth and a 92% prediction-market probability of an earnings beat underpin the bull case. Act now: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just named his top 10 AI stocks — and AMD didn't make the cut. Grab the names FREE today. Sending You to Google News in 3 © iLexx / Getty Images I keep buying Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD | AMD Price Prediction) because agentic AI is rewiring what an AI server needs, and the market still prices AMD like it only sells GPUs. It sells the CPU that runs tool calls, the memory that holds context, and the accelerator that does reasoning. That combination keeps my finger on the buy button. A standard chatbot query is a one-shot GPU pass. An agent is a loop: GPU reasoning, then a CPU tool call or database query, then a KV-cache update, then the next step. The GPU sits idle while the host CPU runs sandboxed Python, hits SQL, and pings legacy microservices. The CPU stops being a background component and becomes the active traffic controller. That is exactly the workload AMD sells into with EPYC plus Instinct plus ROCm, and it is why Lisa Su told investors on the Q1 call that “inferencing and agentic AI drive increasing demand for high-performance CPUs and accelerators.” AMD owns the x86 server CPU franchise that this stack requires, an advantage its accelerator rivals lack. Data Center revenue hit $5.775 billion, up 57% year over year, in Q1 FY2026, and total revenue landed at $10.253 billion, up 37.85%. Free cash flow ran $2.566 billion, a 252.96% jump. Management guided Q2 to roughly $11.2 billion, about 46% growth, with gross margin widening to around 56%. The balance sheet carries net cash, with debt/equity at 0.071, so this cash flow is not servicing leverage. The customer roster: OpenAI selected AMD to deploy 6 gigawatts of GPUs, Meta signed for up to 6 gigawatts of Instinct GPUs, and Oracle is standing up a 50,000-GPU Helios cluster. Reddit’s r/stocks caught it too: the top post this month read, “AMD’s Anthropic and Microsoft deals reinforce that AI infrastructure spending remains strong.” I own some NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA). Jensen Huang said “Agentic AI has arrived, doing productive work, generating real value and scaling rapidly across companies and industries”, and the numbers are staggering: $81.615 billion in Q1 FY2027 revenue, up 85.2%, with 75.0% non-GAAP gross margin. NVIDIA also owns the interconnect story with NVLink and a purpose-built ARM CPU roadmap in Vera Rubin. The problem is the base. NVIDIA is a $5.06 trillion company. AMD is $887.7 billion. NVDA trades at price-to-book of 25.69; AMD sits at 13.77. AMD’s PEG is 1.276, and analysts carry 5 Strong Buy, 37 Buy, and zero Sell ratings. I want the CPU-plus-GPU rack that hyperscalers are diversifying into, at a book multiple roughly half of NVIDIA’s. Trailing P/E is 182. That is rich. U.S. export controls on the MI308 already cost AMD an ~$800 million inventory charge in Q2 2025. What keeps the thesis intact is the forward P/E of 76 against 91.2% quarterly earnings growth, and the fact that current guidance excludes China MI308 revenue entirely. The multiple compresses if execution holds. Polymarket currently prices AMD’s next earnings beat at a 91.5% probability. The 1-year return is 240.18%. I add because the agent loop needs a CPU and a GPU under the same roof, and AMD is the only U.S.-listed name selling both at scale. Contact [email protected] for any questions or corrections. Title: Lara Croft can't catch a break: after delaying one Tomb Raider game, Amazon is delaying another and this one won't show up until 2028
URL: https://www.eurogamer.net/tomb-raider-catalyst-delay-2028
Time Published: 2026-07-24T17:06:13Z
Full Content:
You Winston, you lose some. Lara Croft's big comeback at the hands of Amazon has hit yet another hitch. After TV show setbacks and a delay for Tomb Raider 1 "reimagining" Legacy of Atlantis, Amazon's gaming boss has confirmed yet another delay: Lara's other adventure, Tomb Raider: Catalyst, now won't arrive until some time in 2028. Amazon head of gaming Jeffrey Gattis broke the news in a fairly offhand manner while chatting with The Game Business' Chris Dring. Discussing Amazon's games strategy, and its ambition to create a broad gaming portfolio following the recent relaunch of its Luna streaming platform, Gattis said, "We've obviously announced the two Tomb Raider titles: Atlantis comes 12th February next year and then we'll follow on in 2028 with the next one." Amazon announced a partnership with current Tomb Raider steward Crystal Dynamics back in 2022. However, it wasn't until last December the pair finally revealed the extent of its plans, announcing not one but two Tomb Raider games. The first, Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis - a ground-up remake of the very first Tomb Raider - was originally due this year, but was delayed to February 2027 back in June. Which might help fix some of Eurogamer editor-in-chief Chris Tapsell's concerns that it feels "strangely double-A". As for the second game, Tomb Raider: Catalyst, it's a brand-new entry in the series, flinging Lara Croft toward India for a fresh spot of archaeological adventuring. Catalyst was expected to launch for PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC in 2027 - although, thanks to Gattis, we now know otherwise. It hasn't been the smoothest of starts for Amazon's big Lara Croft revival then, and there's been calamity and controversy elsewhere too. In June, it emerged Legacy of Atlantis was being developed using AI, which Crystal Dynamics director of experience Jeff Adams later claimed helped the team "get to [the] right answers faster". When asked to elaborate, however, the interviewer was shut down by Amazon's PR. As for Amazon Prime's live-action Tomb Raider TV show, filming ground to a halt earlier this year when lead actor Sophie Turner suffered a back injury on set, although shooting has now resumed. Amid all this, Tomb Raider developer Crystal Dynamics has undergone multiple rounds of layoffs. In June it confirmed a fresh wave of cuts impacting 20 staff, making for its fourth round of layoffs in less than a year. The core of my thesis is simple. Hock Tan built a company that sells the picks and shovels the hyperscalers cannot buy anywhere else, and he pairs that with software cash flows from VMware and a dividend I can plan a retirement around. That combination is why I keep clicking buy. Start with the AI engine. Next comes the cash. Q2 free cash flow was $10.26 billion, or 46% of revenue, with an adjusted EBITDA margin of 69%. Full-year FY2025 free cash flow reached $26.91 billion. Cash generation at that scale speaks for itself. Then the dividend. Broadcom has raised its payout 15 consecutive years since fiscal 2011, with the last hike lifting the quarterly to $0.65, a 10% increase. That is the kind of streak I plan a retirement withdrawal schedule around. Every reader lands first on NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) or Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) when they think AI chips. I keep landing here instead because Broadcom sells something distinct from NVIDIA’s lineup: custom ASICs designed to spec for individual hyperscalers, plus the networking silicon that stitches those clusters together. The Apple relationship, reported by retail as a $30B+ custom AI chip deal through 2031, is the template. Add a Semiconductor Solutions segment growing 79% year-over-year and an Infrastructure Software segment producing $7.18 billion of high-margin recurring revenue, and I own a business model neither pure GPU maker offers, with a dividend streak neither matches. Customer concentration is real. Broadcom itself flags dependence on a limited number of large customers and significant indebtedness. If one hyperscaler cuts its custom ASIC roadmap, a quarter gets ugly fast. I stay because free cash flow of $10.26 billion in a single quarter services the debt with room to spare, and cash on the balance sheet grew to $19.63 billion, up 107.22% year-over-year. That is defense I can live with. Shares closed at $386.50 on July 21, roughly 6% off the 52-week high of $494.18. The Wall Street consensus target sits at $524.51 with 44 buys against 4 holds and zero sells. The base-case fair value modeled at $404.96 is my accumulation ceiling. Under that number, my finger stays on the buy button. Above it, I let the dividend do the work. The pivot back in is back on because Broadcom is compounding cash at hyperscaler speed while paying me a raise every year. I will keep buying until the price catches up to the business, and then I will keep holding while the business keeps running ahead. Contact [email protected] for any questions or corrections.
